content.text:
Annual Review 1 covered the period 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025 for FCDO-funded programme MWI-EDU-AR-4471. The approved FCDO contribution was GBP 1,240,000. Submitted partner returns used a different review window, from 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25, and finance had not yet been recut to the award-letter period. This created a reporting limitation for this summary, but the available evidence still showed that Year 1 delivery remained broadly on track.

Progress against plan was mixed but generally positive. Re-enrolment or new retention reached 684 girls against the Year 1 target of 650, and this was recorded as score A. Attendance at 80% or more reached 472 against the Year 1 target of 500, recorded as score B; late attendance registers from four schools affected this result. WASH delivery also advanced ahead of the Year 1 milestone on latrine rehabilitation, with 31 girls' latrine stances delivered against a target of 24 and recorded as score A.

Across output indicators with available actuals and endline targets, implementation showed substantial delivery in Year 1: 684 girls were re-enrolled or newly retained against an endline target of 1,200; 472 girls attended at least 80% of school days against a target of 900; and 438 girls completed at least 20 remedial learning sessions against a target of 850. On school environment and support measures, the programme reported 31 latrine stances rehabilitated or newly functional against a target of 40; 17 schools with menstrual health supplies and trained focal teachers against a target of 40; 392 caregivers received education hardship grants against a target of 800; and 571 girls received school re-entry kits or learning materials against a target of 1,100. Follow-up verification for hardship grant households reached 0.68 against an endline target recorded as either 0.85 in the logframe export or 85% in the proposal; these appear to refer to the same threshold in different formats, but the format should be confirmed in final review. The programme also held 3 district learning meetings against a target of 8 and trained 136 school and community actors on girls' re-entry and safeguarding protocols against a target of 240.

Financial delivery across sampled output lines totalled GBP 694,860 against forecast GBP 653,000. Variance was not uniform. OP1.1 spent GBP 174,850 against budget GBP 162,000, with increased lake-shore transport costs reported. OP2.1 spent GBP 148,900 against budget GBP121,000 while exceeding its Year milestone on latrine stances delivered. Some lines underspent where delivery was incomplete: OP2.2 spent GBP39,600 against budget GBP42,000 and remained below the Year milestone because menstrual health supply delays affected delivery in only seventeen of twenty schools.

No new material risks were reported beyond those already captured in the grant risk register. Safeguarding referral pathways were tested in supported schools, and monitoring returns did not report any major incident trend during Year. An operational assumption held in most schools: focal teachers were available for implementation. However, three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training, which contributed to slower progress on OP2.2. There was also no evidence that funds were used other than intended; hardship grant checks removed duplicate records for sixteen caregivers before payment.

The evidence base for this review drew on school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists and district validation samples. District validation confirmed re-entry figures. No standalone external evaluation was commissioned in Year; monitoring relied on termly indicator returns and partner spot checks.

Actions already agreed from this review were clear: recut finance and reporting to the FCDO review window of fifteen October to fourteen October; secure late Term  attendance registers from four schools; complete menstrual health training in the three remaining schools; finish disposal bins linked to four latrine units; and close the remaining OP2.2 gap.

content.text:
Performance against the outcome objective was positive overall, with Year 1 delivery broadly on track against the agreed results framework. Monitoring used term attendance registers and school safeguarding pathway checks, and supported girls’ attendance and retention improved against Year 1 milestones, with variance notes recorded in the AR1 export. Progress at output level was mixed but generally satisfactory.

Under Output 1, re-enrolment and retention performed strongly. OP1.1 reached 684 girls re-enrolled or newly retained against a Year 1 target of 650, and OP1.2 reached 472 girls attending at least 80% of school days against a Year 1 target of 500. OP1.3 recorded 438 girls completing at least 20 remedial learning sessions against an endline target of 850; submitted records did not provide the Year 1 milestone in the confirmed fact set for this section, so assessment is based on actual delivery only. Evidence for these results came from school registers, re-entry club forms and district validation samples. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures, while late attendance register submission from four schools affected attendance reporting. Previous review actions on register cleaning were partially complete, and September deduplication removed double-count risk on OP1.1.

Under Output 2, physical access and menstrual health support advanced but not evenly across all schools. OP2.1 delivered 31 girls’ latrine stances rehabilitated or newly functional against a Year 1 target of 24, which indicated stronger-than-planned infrastructure progress during the period. By contrast, OP2.2 reached 17 schools with menstrual health supplies and trained focal teachers against a Year 1 target of 20. The main reason for variance was delay in menstrual health supplies, alongside the fact that three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training. WASH engineer certificates formed part of the evidence base for this output area.

Under Output 3, direct support to households and girls progressed close to planned Year 1 levels on some indicators but remained below endline totals overall, which is expected at this stage of implementation. OP3.1 reached 392 caregivers receiving an education hardship grant against a Year 1 target of 400, and OP3.2 reached 571 girls receiving a school re-entry kit or learning materials against a Year 1 target of 550. For follow-up quality, OP3.3 recorded an actual value of 0.68 against an endline target recorded as either 0.85 in the logframe export or 85% in the proposal; these appear to describe the same quantity in different formats, but format confirmation was not available in submitted records. Mobile-money hardship grant lists supported verification, and no evidence showed funds being used other than as intended; hardship grant processes deduplicated 16 caregiver records before payment.

Under Output 4, system-level engagement also progressed but remained uneven across indicators captured in the current logframe export. OP4.1 recorded 3 district learning meetings with documented action points against a Year 1 target of 4, while OP4.3 reached 136 school and community actors trained on girls’ re-entry and safeguarding protocols against a Year 1 target of 120. The partner reported that district learning meetings were held with documented action points, and these meetings contributed to routine review of delivery constraints.

Financial delivery across sampled output lines was higher than forecast during the period: actual spend totalled GBP 694,860 against forecast GBP 653,000. Variance appeared concentrated in some lines where delivery moved faster or costs rose above plan, including lake-shore transport costs affecting OP1.1 and higher actual spend than budget on OP2.1. At the same time, some lines underspent where activities lagged, including OP3.3 and OP4.1. This pattern suggested active delivery rather than broad implementation slowdown.

The main issues affecting performance were operational rather than strategic. No new material risks were reported beyond those already captured in the grant risk register, no major climate shock stopped delivery in Year 1, safeguarding referral pathways were tested in supported schools, and no major incident trend was reported in monitoring returns. The clearest shortfalls were concentrated in attendance reporting delays and incomplete menstrual health coverage in three remaining schools.

The evidence base was adequate for Annual Review purposes but had clear limitations that should be noted transparently. Indicator actuals were drawn from the BridgeLight AR1 export with source notes per output; attendance and financial lines included variance explanations; monitoring relied on termly indicator returns and partner spot checks rather than a standalone external evaluation in Year 1. There was also a reporting-period inconsistency: partner returns used 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25 while the award letter set AR1 as covering from 2024-10-15 to 2025-10-14, and finance had not recut figures to that formal window.

Overall conclusion: delivery during the period supported progress toward the outcome that girls demonstrate improved retention, attendance and learning continuity with reduced barriers. Performance was strongest where activities depended on direct mobilisation or construction outputs; it was weaker where delivery relied on supply timing or late school-level reporting. The main lesson from the period was that data timeliness and completion conditions at school level mattered as much as activity rollout itself for demonstrating results within the review window.

content.text:
Monitoring in Year 1 relied on routine programme records rather than a standalone external evaluation. Submitted records stated that indicator actuals were drawn from the BridgeLight AR1 export, with source notes per output, and that attendance and financial lines included variance explanations. The evidence base used school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists, and district validation samples. Outcome monitoring used term attendance registers and school safeguarding pathway checks. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures, while partner spot checks supported routine verification.

The available evidence was strongest for output delivery that could be verified through administrative records. Re-entry and retention reporting showed OP1.1 actual achievement of 684 girls against an endline target of 1,200, supported by school registers and re-entry club forms. Attendance reporting showed OP1.2 actual achievement of 472 girls against an endline target of 900, but this line was weaker than re-entry data because four schools submitted attendance registers late. WASH delivery evidence was also relatively strong where physical completion could be checked: OP2.1 reported 31 girls' latrine stances rehabilitated or newly functional against an endline target of 40, with WASH engineer certificates cited as evidence. For cash-linked support, hardship grant records and mobile-money lists supported OP3.1 actual achievement of 392 caregivers against an endline target of 800, and district validation samples provided an additional check on reported delivery.

No standalone external evaluation was commissioned in Year 1. Evaluation activity therefore remained limited to termly indicator returns, partner spot checks, and district validation samples. That meant the review could assess whether outputs were delivered and whether supported girls' attendance and retention improved against Year 1 milestones recorded in the AR1 export, but it could not draw stronger causal conclusions than the submitted monitoring system allowed.

There were material data quality limits that affected confidence in some findings. Partner returns used a review period of 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25, while the award letter stated that the first Annual Review covered 2024-10-15 to 2025-10-14; finance had not yet been recut to that formal FCDO window. This timing mismatch did not invalidate the Year 1 picture, but it reduced precision when aligning narrative, finance and results to the award letter requirements. Attendance data were also incomplete at the point of review because four schools submitted registers late, which affected OP1.2 reporting. In addition, menstrual health supply delays affected OP2.2 performance; submitted gap information noted delivery at 17 out of the planned 20 schools for that stage of implementation, and three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training.

Taken together, the evidence was adequate for an Annual Review judgement on output delivery trends and variance against milestones, especially where administrative or physical verification existed. It was less strong for full-period comparability because of the reporting window mismatch, and less complete for attendance-sensitive indicators because of late school submissions. The review therefore treated reported progress as credible but not equally strong across all indicators.

| Re-entry and retention delivery under OP1.1 | School registers, re-entry club forms, district validation samples | Moderate to strong | Routine monitoring only; no external evaluation cited | Suitable for assessing reported output achievement and milestone variance |

| WASH infrastructure under OP2.1 | WASH engineer certificates | Stronger than self-reported activity data | Evidence spoke to completion status more than sustained use | Appropriate for judging delivered infrastructure outputs |
| Hardship grant support under OP3.1 | Mobile-money hardship grant lists and district validation samples | Moderate to strong | Review relied on administrative records rather than independent outcome verification | Adequate for confirming payment-related delivery figures |

The phrase '17 out of the planned 20 schools for that stage of implementation' restated the human-confirmed gap answer on OP2.2 without inferring any additional programme-wide target beyond what was supplied.

content.text:
During the review period, no new material risks were reported beyond those already recorded in the grant risk register. The main delivery issue that affected implementation was delay in menstrual health supplies, which affected OP2.2 and left delivery at 17 schools against a Year 1 target of 20 schools. This sat alongside an operational assumption that female focal teachers would be available for menstrual health training. That assumption held in most schools, but did not hold in 3 schools, which contributed to slower completion of this activity.

Other delivery risks were managed without stopping implementation. Lake-shore transport costs increased for OP1.1, and this was reflected in spend of GBP 174,850 against a budget of GBP 162,000 on that line. Even with that pressure, OP1.1 still exceeded its Year 1 target: 684 girls were re-enrolled against a target of 650, as recorded in the Annual Review evidence pack. No major climate shock was reported to have stopped delivery in Year 1.

Financial control remained adequate during the period. There was no evidence that funds were used other than as intended. For hardship grants, payment controls identified and removed duplicate entries before transfer: 16 caregiver records were deduplicated before payment. Monitoring and financial review across sampled output lines showed actual spend of GBP 694,860 against forecast spend of GBP 653,000. Variance was present across lines, but submitted records stated that attendance and financial lines included variance explanations.

Safeguarding controls remained active during implementation. Safeguarding referral pathways were tested in supported schools, and Year 1 monitoring returns did not report any major incident trend. Outcome monitoring also used school safeguarding pathway checks alongside term attendance registers. This gave some assurance that safeguarding arrangements were functioning as intended during delivery.

There were, however, data quality and reporting control issues that need to be tracked because they affect assurance over results reporting rather than field safety itself. Partner returns used a review period of 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25, while the award letter set the first Annual Review period as 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025; finance had not yet recut to the formal FCDO window. In addition, 4 schools submitted attendance registers late, which affected OP1.2 reporting. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures, which reduced concern over OP1.1 double counting; submitted updates also noted that September deduplication removed double-count risk on OP1.1.

Overall, risk controls were broadly effective during the period. Delivery continued without any reported new material risk or major climate-related disruption, safeguarding systems were tested and no major incident trend was reported, and financial controls detected duplicate hardship-grant records before payment. The main residual issues were narrower: delayed menstrual health supplies, gaps in availability of female focal teachers in a small number of schools, late attendance registers from 4 schools, and misalignment between partner reporting dates and the formal FCDO review window.
assumptions: Specific previous and current RAG ratings for individual risks were not available in submitted records, so no rated risk table rows were populated.
Specific mitigation owners and status fields for a manual risk register update table were not available in submitted records.
The Year 1 target of 20 schools for OP2.2 came from a human-confirmed gap answer rather than a fact key.
The Year 1 target of 650 girls for OP1.1 came from a human-confirmed gap answer rather than a fact key.

content.text:
Value for Money was assessed against economy, efficiency, effectiveness and equity requirements set out for the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office Annual Review. Across sampled output lines, Year 1 actual spend totalled GBP 694,860 against forecast GBP 653,000. This showed moderate cost pressure overall, but delivery remained broadly on track and several Year 1 milestones were met or exceeded.

Economy. Spending pressures were concentrated in a small number of lines rather than across the full portfolio. OP1.1 spent GBP 174,850 against a budget of GBP 162,000, while OP2.1 spent GBP 148,900 against GBP 121,000. Reported cost drivers explain part of this variance: lake-shore transport costs increased for OP1.1, and no major climate shock stopped delivery in Year 1. Other lines underspent against budget, including OP1.3 at GBP 81,330 against GBP 88,000, OP2.2 at GBP 39,600 against GBP 42,000, OP3.3 at GBP 24,980 against GBP 31,000 and OP4.1 at GBP 32,700 against GBP 39,000. Financial control on transfer-based support was credible: there was no evidence of funds not used as intended, and hardship grant records were deduplicated before payment.

Efficiency. Delivery efficiency was mixed but acceptable for Year 1. Some outputs converted spend into results above milestone pace. Re-enrolment under OP1.1 reached 684 girls against the Year 1 target of 650 despite the transport-related overspend. School sanitation under OP2.1 reached 31 latrine stances against a Year 1 target of 24, again ahead of milestone pace though at higher cost than budgeted. By contrast, attendance under OP1.2 reached 472 girls against a Year 1 target of 500; partner reporting noted that four schools submitted attendance registers late, which affected reported performance rather than indicating confirmed non-delivery across all supported schools. Menstrual health support under OP2.2 also lagged its Year 1 milestone: records noted delays in menstrual health supplies and that three schools lacked a female focal teacher for training.

Effectiveness. Results suggest that expenditure translated into substantive output delivery in most areas linked to retention and re-entry. Girls re-enrolled or newly retained reached 684 against an endline target of 1,200; girls attending at least eighty percent of school days reached 472 against an endline target of 900; girls completing at least twenty remedial learning sessions reached 438 against an endline target of 850; caregivers receiving an education hardship grant reached 392 against an endline target of 800; and girls receiving a school re-entry kit or learning materials reached 571 against an endline target of 1,100. Follow-up verification on hardship grant households stood at 0.68 against an endline target recorded as either 0.85 in the logframe export or eighty-five percent in the proposal source; these appear to describe the same threshold in different formats but should still be confirmed in final review drafting. Governance and local coordination outputs also progressed: district learning meetings reached three against an endline target of eight, and school or community actors trained on girls' re-entry and safeguarding protocols reached one hundred and thirty-six against an endline target of two hundred and forty.

Evidence strength supported a reasonable VfM judgement. Indicator actuals were drawn from the BridgeLight AR1 export with source notes per output line; evidence included school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists and district validation samples. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures. No standalone external evaluation was commissioned in Year 1; monitoring instead relied on termly indicator returns and partner spot checks.

Equity. The programme design included attention to vulnerability through support reaching girls with disabilities, ultra-poor households and out-of-school girls, but submitted records did not provide numeric disaggregation for this section. Equity can therefore only be assessed partially from available evidence. The use of hardship grants, re-entry kits and menstrual health support indicates that resources were directed toward practical barriers to girls' participation and return to school; however, exact shares by vulnerability group were not available in submitted records.

Overall VfM assessment: acceptable with some corrective action needed. Economy was affected by transport costs on OP1.1 and higher-than-budget sanitation costs on OP2.1; efficiency remained reasonable because both lines delivered above Year 1 milestone pace. Effectiveness was strongest on re-enrolment and sanitation outputs and weaker on attendance reporting completeness and menstrual health rollout. Priority changes identified during the review were to recut finance to the FCDO fifteen-October to fourteen-October review window, complete menstrual health training in the three remaining schools within the Year 1 set referenced in monitoring notes, finish disposal bins at four latrine units, and secure late attendance registers from four schools so that VfM judgements rest on complete performance data.
assumptions: Equity assessment was kept qualitative because no numeric gender-age-vulnerability disaggregation beyond broad vulnerability categories was provided in submitted records.
The statement on Year 1 milestones for OP1.1, OP1.2 and OP2.1 relied on confirmed gap answers because milestone values were not consistently available as fact keys for all indicators.

For OP3.3 target presentation, the narrative treated fact values '0.85' and '85%' as likely equivalent formats for the same threshold but flagged this for confirmation rather than asserting a reconciled figure.
Commercial improvement was addressed through financial control and corrective management actions because no separate procurement or supplier performance data were provided.

sections.label: F. Programme Management: Delivery, Commercial and Financial Performance

content.text:
Delivery in the first Annual Review period was broadly on track against Year 1 milestones. Reported progress included 684 girls re-enrolled against a Year 1 target of 650, 472 girls attending at least 80% of school days against a target of 500, and 31 latrine stances delivered against a target of 24. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures, although late register submission from four schools affected attendance reporting. Monitoring evidence drew on school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists and district validation samples.

Financial delivery across sampled output lines in the AR1 export totalled GBP 694,860 against forecast spend of GBP 653,000. Variance at line level was mixed. Overspends were recorded on OP1.1 at GBP 174,850 against GBP 162,000, OP1.2 at GBP 98,740 against GBP 94,000, OP2.1 at GBP 148,900 against GBP 121,000, OP3.1 at GBP 151,440 against GBP 146,000, OP3.2 at GBP 109,250 against GBP 103,000 and OP4.3 at GBP 58,630 against GBP 54,000. Underspends were recorded on OP1.3 at GBP 81,330 against GBP 88,000, OP2.2 at GBP 39,600 against GBP 42,000, OP3.3 at GBP 24,980 against GBP 31,000 and OP4.1 at GBP 32,700 against GBP 39,000.

Available evidence indicates that some spending pressure reflected delivery conditions rather than weak control. Lake-shore transport costs increased for OP1.1. There was no evidence that funds were used other than as intended; hardship grant records were deduplicated before payment and removed duplicate risk in caregiver support lists. District learning meetings were held with documented action points, and FCDO review pack requirements were being managed in line with the award letter.

Commercial and operational issues were limited but not absent. No new material risks beyond those already in the grant risk register were reported during the year. The main delivery issue affecting implementation was delay in menstrual health supplies under OP2.2; reported progress reached 17 schools against the Year 1 milestone of 20 schools. A related operational assumption held in most schools but not all: three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training. No major climate shock stopped delivery in Year 1 monitoring returns.

Management attention remained focused on data quality and alignment with FCDO reporting requirements. Partner returns used a review window of 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25 while the award letter set the first Annual Review period as 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025; finance had not yet recut to that formal window. Previous review actions on register cleaning were only partly complete during the year, but September deduplication reduced double-count risk on OP1.1.

Delivery, commercial and financial performance table:

| Area | Planned position | Actual position | Variance or issue | Management action |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Delivery performance | Year 1 milestones tracked through the AR1 results framework | Delivery remained broadly on track; re-entry and latrine outputs exceeded cited Year 1 milestones while attendance was slightly below milestone | Four schools submitted attendance registers late; this affected attendance reporting | M&E follow-up was identified to secure missing Term records |
| Partner performance | Partner reporting and validation expected through district systems | District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures | Attendance data quality was weaker because four schools reported late | Register cleaning continued and duplicate risk on OP1.1 was reduced through September deduplication |
| Financial delivery | Forecast versus actual expenditure statement required under AR1 obligations | Sampled output-line spend reached GBP 694,860 against forecast GBP 653,000 | Mixed over- and underspend across output lines; finance period labelling did not yet match the award-letter review window | Programme management identified recutting finance to the formal FCDO review period |
| Commercial / procurement issues | Inputs expected to support planned output delivery | Menstrual health supply delays affected OP2.2 delivery to schools | Supply delay contributed to progress of 17 schools against a milestone of 20; three schools also lacked a female focal teacher for training | WASH follow-up was identified to close remaining gaps |
| FCDO management actions | Review pack due to FCDO by the stated deadline with updated logframe and financial statement | District learning meetings were held with documented action points and reporting requirements were being managed against the award letter | Reporting-period mismatch between partner returns and formal AR1 dates remained unresolved during the period | Programme management identified alignment of reporting-period labelling with the award letter as a priority |

Overall, programme management during the period showed acceptable control over delivery and expenditure using available evidence from partner returns and validation samples. The main weaknesses were timing and completeness of some school-level data and incomplete alignment between partner reporting periods and the formal FCDO Annual Review window.
assumptions: No specific information was available on supplier or consultant performance beyond menstrual health supply delays affecting OP2.2; narrative therefore referred to commercial or procurement issues only at a general level.
The table used management actions drawn from confirmed recommendations because separate completed-action records for each issue were not fully available in submitted records.
The section referred to 'sampled output lines' for spend totals because that wording appeared in the confirmed gap answer for financial delivery.

The report-level period is listed as 2025-04-01 to 2026-03-31, but this section used the formal AR1 window where cited because submitted evidence stated that partner returns had not been recut to match it.

content.text:
Recommendations were drawn from Year 1 delivery evidence and from issues that affected performance during the review period. Current review recommendations focused on three corrective actions: recutting finance to the FCDO 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025 review window, completing menstrual health training in the three remaining schools, and securing submission of late attendance registers. These actions responded directly to the reporting-period mismatch noted between partner returns and the award letter, the OP2.2 shortfall linked to supply delays and missing female focal teachers in three schools, and delayed attendance reporting from four schools.

Updates on previous recommendations showed partial progress. Earlier actions on register cleaning were partially completed, and September deduplication removed double-count risk on OP1.1. That was a useful control improvement, but it did not remove all data quality issues because four schools still submitted attendance registers late.

Priorities for the next period were therefore clear and evidence-based: close the OP2.2 gap recorded at 17 out of 20 schools, complete disposal bins at four latrine units, and align reporting-period labelling with the award letter. The agreed action plan assigned responsibility to the Programme Manager to recut the AR1 period by Q1 of the next period, to M&E to follow up with the four schools on Term 3 registers, and to WASH to finish disposal bins.

These recommendations were proportionate to performance during the year. Year 1 delivery remained broadly on track in several areas, including OP1.1 at 684 girls re-enrolled against a Year 1 target of 650 and OP2.1 at 31 latrine stances against a target of 24, so recommended actions concentrated on specific gaps rather than wider redesign.
assumptions: Exact due dates for each action were not available in submitted records; only 'Q1 next period' was provided for recutting the AR1 period.
Table-ready status labels for each recommendation were not provided in submitted records, so narrative refers to progress qualitatively rather than assigning formal status categories.
The required recommendations table could not be fully populated because no source provided complete row-level due dates, priorities, statuses, and follow-up fields for each action.

content.text:
This Annual Review covered the reporting period 2025-04-01 to 2026-03-31 under FCDO-funded programme MWI-EDU-AR-4471. The programme itself ran from 2024-10-15 to 2026-10-14, while the award letter stated that the first formal Annual Review period ran from 2024-10-15 to 2025-10-14. Submitted records therefore indicated a mismatch between the current report period label and the formal Year 1 review dates, and this should be read with that qualification.

At summary level, the programme remained aligned to its stated impact and outcome: adolescent girls in Machinga and Mangochi completing basic education in safer, more supportive learning environments, with improved retention, attendance and learning continuity and fewer practical and safeguarding barriers. However, verified actual results for the reporting period were not available in the submitted evidence pack used for this section. As a result, overall progress could not be rated here against output or outcome targets with confidence.

The approved FCDO contribution was GBP 1,240,000. The results framework set clear targets across attendance, retention, remedial learning, hardship support, menstrual health and hygiene support, safeguarding systems, learning products and district engagement. These included targets of 1,200 girls re-enrolled or newly retained, 900 supported girls attending at least 80% of school days in the last term, 850 girls completing at least 20 remedial learning sessions, 800 caregivers receiving a hardship grant linked to attendance, 1,100 girls receiving a re-entry kit or learning materials, 40 lockable girls' latrine stances rehabilitated or functional, 40 schools with menstrual supplies and trained focal teachers, 40 schools with an active safeguarding referral pathway tested, 8 district learning meetings with documented action points, 5 learning briefs produced and shared with stakeholders, and 240 school or community actors trained on re-entry and safeguarding. Outcome-level targets were also set at 70% for supported girls attending at least 80% of days in the last term, 65% progressing to the next grade or a re-entry pathway, and 72% reporting that school was safe during menstruation and travel.

The main issue for this section was not necessarily lack of programme activity but lack of verified performance data in the material provided here. The template required an Annual Review narrative, output scoring using the five-point system with evidence, a maintained logframe or equivalent results framework, and disaggregated monitoring data by gender, age and vulnerability where relevant. Those requirements were clear from the award documentation. Yet no confirmed output scores, actual indicator values, review team details or risk rating were available in the source set used for this summary. Exact disaggregation for girls with disabilities, ultra-poor households or out-of-school status was also not available here; the related equity reach indicator had no numeric target recorded.

On that basis, this summary recorded a cautious position. The programme had an approved scope, timeframe and target architecture in place, but this section could not confirm delivery against plan during 2025-04-01 to 2026-03-31 using verified actuals. The immediate recommendation was therefore to reconcile the reporting period basis with the formal Annual Review cycle stated in the award letter and complete the review pack with evidenced actual results, output scores, risk information and required disaggregation before final submission to FCDO.

content.text:
During the reporting period 2025-04-01 to 2026-03-31, the programme remained aligned to its stated outcome: adolescent girls targeted demonstrate improved school retention, attendance and learning continuity, with reduced practical and safeguarding barriers. The longer-term impact remained that adolescent girls in Machinga and Mangochi complete basic education in safer, more supportive learning environments. Reporting was prepared within the FCDO Annual Review framework for grant reference MWI-EDU-AR-4471.

Performance against expected results could only be assessed in a limited way from the submitted record. The available evidence confirmed the programme’s intended results framework and target values for key outcome and output indicators, but it did not include verified actual values for outcome indicators within this section’s source material. As a result, progress against the outcome could not be scored quantitatively here without overstating what the evidence showed.

The logframe direction of travel was clear. Outcome targets were set at 70% for supported girls attending at least 80% of school days in the last term, 65% for progression to the next grade or a re-entry pathway, and 72% for girls reporting that school was safe during menstruation and travel. Output targets also set the expected scale of delivery: 1,200 girls re-enrolled or newly retained; 900 girls attending at least 80% of school days in the last term; 850 girls completing at least 20 remedial learning sessions; 40 lockable girls’ latrine stances rehabilitated or functional; 40 schools with menstrual supplies and trained focal teachers; 40 schools with an active safeguarding referral pathway tested; 800 caregivers receiving a hardship grant linked to attendance; 1,100 girls receiving a re-entry kit or learning materials; 85% of hardship households receiving verified follow-up within 45 days; 8 district learning meetings with documented action points; 5 learning briefs produced and shared with stakeholders; and 240 school or community actors trained on re-entry and safeguarding.

These targets showed that delivery was designed to combine retention support, remedial learning, practical assistance, safer school conditions, safeguarding systems and district-level learning. That package remained coherent with the outcome statement. However, major deviations from expected results could not be confirmed from this evidence set because actual achievements, milestone tracking and verified variance explanations were not available in the submitted material used for this section.

On disaggregation, the award requirements stated that monitoring data must be disaggregated by gender, age and vulnerability. The proposal material also referenced reach to girls with disabilities, ultra-poor girls and out-of-school girls, but no numeric target was stated for that equity measure in the available record. The section therefore cannot report achieved disaggregation or equity reach figures with confidence. Exact disaggregation was not available in submitted records used here.

In conclusion, the programme had a clearly defined outcome pathway and a documented set of annual review obligations under FCDO requirements, including maintenance of a logframe or equivalent results framework and provision of output scoring with evidence. Based on the evidence available for this section, it is reasonable to conclude that performance management arrangements were specified, but actual progress against expected results during this reporting period was not evidenced strongly enough here to support a firm judgement on achievement level. The main lesson from this review stage is straightforward: future performance conclusions should draw directly on verified actuals, milestone status, output scores and disaggregated monitoring data so that variance against targets can be explained transparently.

content.text:
During the reporting period, the evidence base available for this Annual Review was limited and largely procedural rather than performance-focused. The programme operated within FCDO’s requirement to maintain a logframe or equivalent results framework, provide output scoring and evidence, and submit disaggregated monitoring data where relevant. However, the records provided for this section did not include verified indicator actuals, milestone tracking, or completed evaluation products that would allow a stronger assessment of progress against the results framework.

The strongest confirmed evidence in submitted records related to programme design parameters and reporting requirements rather than achieved results. The award documentation confirmed the formal reporting window for the first Annual Review as 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025, while this draft report covered 2025-04-01 to 2026-03-31. That mismatch reduced confidence in assessing whether evidence had been assembled against the correct contractual review cycle. The same award documentation also confirmed that FCDO could request supporting documentation, which reinforced the expectation that underlying records should be available even where they were not included in the material reviewed for this section.

The existing results framework set out clear intended measures for attendance, progression or re-entry, safety, remedial learning, hardship support, school WASH and safeguarding conditions, and learning dissemination. For example, proposal targets referred to girls attending at least 80% of days in the last term, girls completing at least 20 remedial learning sessions, caregivers receiving hardship grants linked to attendance, schools with menstrual supplies and trained focal teachers, schools with tested safeguarding referral pathways, district learning meetings with documented action points, and learning briefs shared with stakeholders. These targets showed that an evaluable framework had been defined. Even so, no corresponding actual values were supplied in the records used here. As a result, this review could comment on evaluability but not on achieved performance.

On evidence quality, there was enough documentation to confirm that indicators and reporting obligations existed; there was not enough to verify delivery levels or outcome change. Evidence quality was therefore mixed: adequate for confirming planned indicators and compliance expectations, weak for judging actual results during the period under review. This mattered most for outcome-level assessment. Outcome statements referred to improved retention, attendance and learning continuity for adolescent girls in Machinga and Mangochi within safer and more supportive learning environments, but no monitored outcome values were available here to test whether those changes had occurred.

No new evaluation findings were evidenced in the submitted material reviewed for this section. Although the Annual Review pack was expected to include any evaluation or learning outputs, none were available in usable form within the present record set. For that reason, there was no basis to assess methodological quality of an evaluation study, triangulate monitoring data with independent inquiry, or judge whether emerging lessons had been validated beyond routine programme reporting.

Data quality limitations were significant. First, indicator actuals were absent across both output and outcome measures cited in programme documents. Second, while disaggregated monitoring data by gender, age and vulnerability was an explicit requirement, no disaggregated dataset or summary table was available in submitted records for this section. Third, one reporting-cycle reference in the award material mentioned an informal October-to-September convention, while the same document set out a formal first Annual Review period ending on 14 October 2025; this required careful handling and reduced certainty about which evidence window some internal references may have followed.

Taken together, the evidence base supported only a cautious conclusion: the programme had a defined theory of change and indicator structure acceptable for review purposes, but this section did not contain sufficient verified monitoring or evaluation material to substantiate claims on delivery quality or results achieved during 2025-04-01 to 2026-03-31.

During the reporting period 2025-04-01 to 2026-03-31, risk reporting for the FCDO-funded programme MWI-EDU-AR-4471 was prepared against the Annual Review requirements set out in the award documentation. The programme maintained a logframe or equivalent results framework, and FCDO’s requirements included output scoring with supporting evidence, disaggregated monitoring data, and access to supporting documentation on request.

Submitted records did not provide a verified risk register update for this section. As a result, this review could not confirm which risks newly emerged, which assumptions materialised, or whether any individual risk rating changed during the period. It also could not present evidenced previous and current RAG ratings for the required risk update table without creating unsupported entries.

Safeguarding remained a core control issue within programme design and delivery. This was reflected in the results framework through targets linked to schools with active safeguarding referral pathways tested and school or community actors trained on re-entry and safeguarding. The outcome framework also tracked girls’ reported safety during menstruation and travel. These features showed that safeguarding risks were recognised within programme architecture. However, the submitted material for this section did not include confirmed incident data, trend analysis, case outcomes, or a documented statement on whether safeguarding risks increased, reduced, or remained stable over the review period.

The same evidence gap applied to fiduciary risk. No verified narrative was available on risks of funds not being used as intended, any control breaches identified during implementation, or corrective action taken during the period under review. Likewise, no confirmed section-specific evidence was provided on climate or environmental risk affecting delivery in Machinga and Mangochi.

Control expectations were clearer than control performance in the records available for drafting. FCDO required disaggregated monitoring data by gender, age and vulnerability where relevant, and retained the right to request supporting documents. Those requirements provided an accountability framework for oversight. Even so, exact evidence on compliance during this reporting period was not available in the submitted records for this section.

Overall, this section should be read as a constrained account based on award-level requirements and results-framework references rather than a fully evidenced risk update. A complete Annual Review narrative would require the underlying risk register, safeguarding reporting summary, and documented management actions from the reporting period.

content.text:
During the reporting period 2025-04-01 to 2026-03-31, programme management reporting for FCDO grant MWI-EDU-AR-4471 was framed against the formal award period from 2024-10-15 to 2026-10-14 and the requirement to submit an Annual Review pack, maintain a logframe or equivalent results framework, provide output scoring with evidence, and hold supporting documentation available on request. The submitted record therefore shows that management attention was directed to delivery assurance, results tracking and compliance with FCDO review requirements.

On delivery performance, the available evidence confirms the programme’s intended Impact and Outcome in Machinga and Mangochi, but it does not provide verified implementation data on partner performance, supplier or consultant performance, or completed activities during this section’s reporting window. Because actual delivery figures were not available in submitted records for this section, performance could not be tested here against output targets such as 1,200 girls re-enrolled or newly retained, 900 girls attending at least 80% of school days, 850 girls completing remedial sessions, 40 latrine stances rehabilitated or functional, 40 schools with menstrual supplies and trained focal teachers, 40 schools with tested safeguarding referral pathways, 800 caregivers receiving hardship grants, 1,100 girls receiving re-entry kits or learning materials, 8 district learning meetings, 5 learning briefs and 240 school or community actors trained. The same limitation applied to outcome-level targets on attendance, progression or re-entry, and perceived safety.

On financial performance, the only confirmed financial figure in the record was the approved FCDO contribution of GBP 1,240,000. No forecast-versus-actual spend data, burn rate data or variance analysis for the reporting period was available in the submitted evidence for this section. As a result, this review could not confirm whether expenditure tracked to plan during 2025-04-01 to 2026-03-31 or whether any underspend or overspend required corrective action.

On commercial performance, no verified procurement record, contract management update or supplier issue log was available in the evidence provided for this section. It was therefore not possible to confirm whether any commercial issues arose during implementation or whether supplier performance affected delivery.

On management actions and compliance with donor requirements, the record did show clear FCDO expectations: an Annual Review pack was due by 2025-11-21; monitoring data was expected to be disaggregated by gender, age and vulnerability; outputs were to be scored using a five-point system with supporting evidence; and FCDO retained the right to request supporting documents. These requirements established the management standard for the period. However, exact actions taken by FCDO or by implementing partners in response to delivery or financial issues were not evidenced in the material supplied for this section.

Overall, this section can confirm the programme’s management and accountability framework but cannot yet provide a fully evidenced judgement on delivery efficiency, commercial performance or financial execution for the reporting period because actual management data was not included in the submitted records.

content.text:
This Annual Review covered Year 1 delivery under FCDO programme code MWI-EDU-AR-4471. The award letter defined the first Annual Review period as 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025, although partner returns used 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25 and finance had not yet recut to the FCDO review window. The programme remained broadly on track against its Year 1 plan and continued to contribute to the intended outcome that girls demonstrate improved retention, attendance and learning continuity.

Results were mixed but positive overall. Re-enrolment and retention exceeded plan: OP1.1 reached 684 girls against a Year 1 target of 650. Remedial learning also exceeded target, with 438 girls completing at least 20 sessions against a target of 420. Attendance at 80% or more reached 472 girls against a target of 500, below milestone because four schools submitted attendance registers late. Under the safer school environment output, rehabilitation of separate lockable girls' latrine stances exceeded target, with 31 completed against a target of 24. However, schools with menstrual health supplies and trained focal teachers reached 17 against a target of 20; records attributed this shortfall to menstrual health supply delays, and three schools lacked a female focal teacher for training.

Household support largely met planned levels. Education hardship grants reached 392 caregivers against a target of 400, while school re-entry kits or learning materials reached 571 girls against a target of 550. Follow-up verification within 45 days for hardship grant households reached 0.68 against a target of 0.75, so case management did not keep pace with grant delivery in all cases during the review period. System strengthening outputs were also close to plan: district learning meetings reached 3 against a target of 4, while training on girls' re-entry and safeguarding protocols exceeded plan at 136 school and community actors against a target of 120.

Evidence for reported results came from school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists, and district validation samples. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures, and monitoring relied on termly indicator returns and partner spot checks rather than a standalone external evaluation in Year 1. Safeguarding referral pathways were tested in supported schools, with no major incident trend reported in Year 1 monitoring returns. No new material risks were reported beyond those already captured in the grant risk register. There was also no evidence that funds were used other than as intended; hardship grant checks deduplicated 16 caregiver records before payment.

Financial delivery ran slightly above forecast across sampled output lines in the AR1 export: actual spend totalled GBP 694,860 against forecast GBP 653,000. Variance appears linked in part to higher lake-shore transport costs under OP1.1 and stronger-than-planned delivery on several outputs.

Agreed follow-up actions were clear. The Programme Manager was to recut AR1 reporting to the FCDO review window by Q1 of the next period; M&E was to secure missing Term 3 registers from four schools; and WASH was to close the remaining OP2.2 gap, including completion of disposal bins at four latrine units and menstrual health training in the three remaining schools.

content.text:
The programme’s stated outcome was that girls demonstrate improved retention, attendance and learning continuity. During the review period, outcome monitoring used term attendance registers and school safeguarding pathway checks. Reported results showed improvement against Year 1 milestones, with stronger performance on retention and mixed performance on attendance and selected enabling outputs.

Progress against expected results was broadly on track. Under Output 1, 684 girls were re-enrolled or retained against a Year 1 target of 650. Attendance at 80% or more of school days reached 472 against a target of 500, while 438 girls completed at least 20 remedial learning sessions against a target of 420. This pattern suggested that re-entry and remedial support were delivered at or above plan, but regular attendance lagged behind target.

Under Output 2, delivery on safer and more supportive school conditions was mixed. The programme rehabilitated 31 separate lockable girls’ latrine stances against a target of 24. By contrast, 17 schools had menstrual health supplies and trained focal teachers against a target of 20. The reported shortfall was linked to menstrual health supply delays. A related assumption held in most schools, but three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training.

Under Output 3, direct support to households and girls largely tracked close to plan. The programme reached 392 caregivers with an education hardship grant against a target of 400, and 571 girls received a school re-entry kit or learning materials against a target of 550. However, verified attendance follow-up within 45 days reached 0.68 against a target of 0.75, showing weaker case follow-up than planned.

Under Output 4, district and community systems also showed mixed progress. Three district learning meetings were held with documented action points against a target of four, while 136 school or community actors were trained on girls re-entry and safeguarding protocols against a target of 120. Safeguarding referral pathways were tested in supported schools, and Year 1 monitoring returns did not report any major incident trend.

Taken together, these results supported the conclusion that delivery contributed to the outcome objective, especially through stronger re-enrolment or retention performance, remedial participation, school infrastructure rehabilitation, material support to girls, and training of school and community actors. The main areas where performance fell below milestone were attendance at the expected threshold, menstrual health coverage in schools, verified follow-up after hardship grants, and the number of district learning meetings completed.

The main deviations were explained in the available evidence. Four schools submitted attendance registers late, which affected OP1.2 reporting. Menstrual health supply delays reduced OP2.2 delivery to 17 of the planned 20 schools. No new material risks beyond those already recorded in the grant risk register were reported, although lake-shore transport costs increased for OP1.1. No major climate shock stopped delivery in Year 1.

Evidence for this assessment was adequate for routine annual review purposes but had limits. Indicator actuals were drawn from the BridgeLight AR1 export with source notes per output, and evidence included school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists, and district validation samples. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures. No standalone external evaluation was commissioned in Year 1; monitoring relied on termly indicator returns and partner spot checks.

There were also data quality issues that affect interpretation. Partner returns used a review period of 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25 while the award letter cited 15-Oct-2024 to 14-Oct-2025 for the first Annual Review period; finance had not recut the period at the time of reporting. This means trend interpretation should be read as broadly indicative of Year 1 performance rather than as a fully aligned review window.

Overall, performance was credible and mostly positive for Year 1. Delivery exceeded several annual milestones and remained close to plan on others, but weaker attendance reporting and incomplete menstrual health coverage limited progress toward the full outcome standard during the period.

content.text:
Monitoring during the review period relied on routine programme records rather than a standalone evaluation. Indicator actuals were drawn from the BridgeLight AR1 export, with source notes recorded per output, and the evidence base included school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists, and district validation samples. Monitoring also relied on termly indicator returns and partner spot checks. This provided a usable basis for reviewing delivery against the logframe, and submitted records supported assessment of both results and spending at output level.

The evidence was strongest where administrative records could be checked against more than one source. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures, and financial lines in the AR1 export included budget-to-actual comparisons. Submitted records therefore gave reasonable assurance for several Year 1 output claims, including OP1.1 at 684 against a target of 650, OP2.1 at 31 against a target of 24, and OP4.3 at 136 against a target of 120. They also showed areas where performance was below milestone: OP1.2 reached 472 against a target of 500, OP2.2 reached 17 against a target of 20, OP3.1 reached 392 against a target of 400, OP3.3 reached 0.68 against a target of 0.75, and OP4.1 reached 3 against a target of 4.

Evidence quality was weaker for attendance-related reporting than for re-entry or infrastructure outputs. Four schools submitted attendance registers late, which affected OP1.2 reporting. The records still indicated that supported girls' attendance and retention improved against Year 1 milestones, using term attendance registers and school safeguarding pathway checks, but this part of the assessment carried more uncertainty than indicators supported by complete administrative records.

There was also an unresolved reporting-period issue in the submitted evidence pack. Partner returns used 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25, while the award letter cited an Annual Review window from 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025; finance had not recut the period at the time of reporting. That mismatch did not invalidate the Year 1 results set, but it limited strict comparability with the FCDO review window and should be taken into account when reading both performance and expenditure figures.

No standalone external evaluation was commissioned in Year 1. As a result, this section draws conclusions from monitoring evidence rather than from an independent effectiveness study. Within that limitation, the submitted records were sufficient to support a cautious assessment that delivery remained broadly on track overall, with clear shortfalls concentrated in attendance reporting follow-up and menstrual health supply coverage.
assumptions: No baseline or methodological rating scale for evidence quality was provided in submitted records, so evidence quality has been described narratively rather than scored.
The section refers to Year 1 output indicators recorded in the AR1 export because no separate evidence dataset for the stated report period of 2025-04-01 to 2026-03-31 was supplied.
Exact gender, age, or vulnerability disaggregation was not available in submitted records for this section despite the reporting obligation on disaggregated monitoring data.

content.text:
During the period, no new material risks were reported beyond those already captured in the grant risk register. The main delivery issue that materialised affected OP2.2: menstrual health supply delays contributed to performance of 17 schools reached against a target of 20. This shortfall aligned with a related assumption that focal teachers would be available in supported schools. That assumption held in most schools, but three schools did not have a female focal teacher available for menstrual health training during the period. These factors help explain why OP2.2 lagged while other output areas remained broadly on track.

Climate and operating conditions did not stop implementation in Year 1, although they did affect cost pressure. Lake-shore transport costs increased for OP1.1, and this sat alongside actual spend of GBP 174,850 against a budget of GBP 162,000 for that line. Even with that pressure, OP1.1 still exceeded its Year 1 target, reaching 684 girls re-enrolled or retained against a target of 650. This suggests that mitigation measures maintained delivery despite higher operating costs.

Financial control findings during the period were stable. Monitoring and payment controls found no evidence that funds were used other than as intended. For hardship grants, the programme deduplicated 16 caregiver records before payment, which reduced the risk of duplicate disbursement and showed that pre-payment checks were functioning. More broadly, Year 1 actual spend across sampled output lines totalled GBP 694,860 against forecast spend of GBP 653,000 in the AR1 export, so cost control will need continued attention alongside delivery performance.

Safeguarding controls remained active during the reporting period. Safeguarding referral pathways were tested in supported schools, and Year 1 monitoring returns did not report any major incident trend. Training and system-strengthening activity also progressed: 136 school and community actors were trained on girls' re-entry and safeguarding protocols against a target of 120, and district learning meetings reached 3 against a target of 4 with documented action points. These measures supported oversight and case handling, even though exact incident disaggregation was not available in the submitted records.

The section's main control issues were therefore operational rather than systemic: delayed menstrual health inputs, uneven availability of female focal teachers in three schools, higher transport costs linked to lake-shore delivery routes, and routine data quality pressures already noted elsewhere in the review process. Overall, controls remained in place and were used: referral pathways were tested, payment lists were cleaned before transfer, and district validation samples confirmed key re-entry figures.

content.text:
Value for Money was assessed against economy, efficiency, effectiveness and equity using the AR1 export and confirmed monitoring notes. Year 1 actual spend on sampled output lines totalled GBP 694,860 against a forecast of GBP 653,000, so delivery ran above forecast overall. The main cost pressure noted in submitted records was increased lake-shore transport costs affecting OP1.1. At the same time, there was no evidence that funds were used other than intended, and hardship grant controls removed duplicate risk by deduplicating 16 caregiver records before payment.

On economy, the programme showed mixed performance. Some lines underspent against budget, including OP1.3 at GBP 81,330 against GBP 88,000, OP2.2 at GBP 39,600 against GBP 42,000, OP3.3 at GBP 24,980 against GBP 31,000 and OP4.1 at GBP 32,700 against GBP 39,000. Other lines overspent: OP1.1 reached GBP 174,850 against GBP 162,000; OP1.2 reached GBP 98,740 against GBP 94,000; OP2.1 reached GBP 148,900 against GBP 121,000; OP3.1 reached GBP 151,440 against GBP 146,000; OP3.2 reached GBP 109,250 against GBP 103,000; and OP4.3 reached GBP 58,630 against GBP 54,000. The largest variance sat on OP2.1. That overspend accompanied delivery above target, with 31 latrine stances rehabilitated against a target of 24. This suggests higher unit cost than planned but stronger physical delivery during the period.

On efficiency, several outputs converted spending into results at or above milestone level. OP1.1 achieved 684 girls re-enrolled or retained against a target of 650 despite transport cost pressure and after register cleaning reduced double-count risk. OP1.3 achieved 438 girls completing at least 20 remedial learning sessions against a target of 420 while spending below budget. OP3.2 reached 571 girls receiving school re-entry kits or learning materials against a target of 550 with moderate overspend relative to budget. OP4.3 trained 136 school or community actors against a target of 120.

Efficiency was weaker where delivery bottlenecks slowed conversion of inputs into results. OP1.2 reached 472 girls attending at least 80% of school days against a target of 500; four schools submitted attendance registers late, which affected reporting completeness for this indicator. OP2.2 reached only 17 schools against a target of 20 because menstrual health supply delays affected implementation and three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training. OP3.3 also fell short: verified attendance follow-up within 45 days reached a proportion of 0.68 against a target of 0.75.

On effectiveness, Year 1 delivery remained broadly on track and outcome monitoring reported improved attendance and retention for supported girls against Year 1 milestones. Results were strongest on re-entry support and school environment improvements: re-enrolment or retention exceeded target by reaching 684 girls; remedial learning exceeded target at 438 girls; latrine rehabilitation exceeded target at 31 stances; re-entry kits or learning materials exceeded target at reaching an additional group above the Year 1 milestone; and training on girls' re-entry and safeguarding protocols also surpassed plan at 136 participants compared with the target of120 . These gains supported the programme outcome that girls demonstrated improved retention, attendance and learning continuity.

Effectiveness was moderated by shortfalls in attendance consistency and menstrual health support coverage. Attendance at the eighty per cent threshold remained below plan, district learning meetings reached three against a target of four, and hardship grant follow-up did not meet the expected verification rate within forty-five days. No new material risks beyond those in the grant risk register were reported during the period, no major climate shock stopped delivery in Year
0Year
01 monitoring returns recorded no major incident trend.

On equity, available evidence showed that support channels were directed toward barriers that commonly affect girls' participation: hardship grants to caregivers reached392 households against a target of400; school re-entry kits or learning materials reached571 girls against a target of550; separate lockable girls' latrine stances were rehabilitated; menstrual health supplies and trained focal teachers were in place in17 schools; and safeguarding referral pathways were tested in supported schools with no major incident trend reported in Year
01 monitoring returns. However, submitted records did not provide quantified disaggregation by age or vulnerability for this section even though disaggregated monitoring data was an FCDO reporting requirement.

Overall, Value for Money was acceptable but uneven across outputs in Year
01. The programme generated strong output delivery on several lines despite moderate overspend overall on sampled outputs and specific cost pressure on transport and WASH works. The clearest improvements needed were to align finance reporting to the FCDO review window of15 October2024 to14 October2025, close the remaining gap on OP2.2 by completing menstrual health training in the three remaining schools and finishing disposal bins at four latrine units, and secure late attendance registers so that efficiency and effectiveness judgements rest on complete evidence.

Equity assessment relied on proxy evidence from hardship grants, re-entry kits, menstrual health support and safeguarding measures because quantified age or vulnerability disaggregation was not available in submitted records for this section.

sections.label: F. Programme Management: Delivery, Commercial and Financial Performance

content.text:
Delivery in Year 1 remained broadly on track, with stronger performance on several output lines and some reporting and implementation issues that need follow-up. Re-entry and retention delivery exceeded plan: OP1.1 reached 684 girls against a Year 1 target of 650. Remedial learning also exceeded target, with 438 girls completing at least 20 sessions against a target of 420. School re-entry kits or learning materials reached 571 girls against a target of 550, and training on girls' re-entry and safeguarding protocols reached 136 school and community actors against a target of 120. WASH infrastructure delivery was ahead of plan on latrine rehabilitation, with 31 separate lockable girls' latrine stances completed against a target of 24.

Performance was weaker on a smaller set of indicators. Attendance at 80% or more reached 472 girls against a target of 500. Partner reporting confirmed that late attendance registers from four schools affected OP1.2 reporting. Menstrual health support reached 17 schools against a target of 20. Submitted risk information stated that menstrual health supply delays affected this result, and that three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training. Hardship grant delivery was close to plan at 392 caregivers against a target of 400, but verified attendance follow-up within 45 days reached 0.68 against a target of 0.75. District learning meetings also fell slightly short, with three meetings held against a target of four.

Partner performance was mixed but acceptable overall. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures, which supported confidence in OP1.1 results. At the same time, late register submission from four schools reduced the completeness of attendance reporting. Previous actions on register cleaning were only partly complete, although September deduplication removed double-count risk on OP1.1 and hardship grant checks removed duplicated caregiver records before payment.

Financial delivery ran above forecast across the sampled output lines in the AR1 export. Actual spend totalled GBP 694,860 against forecast spend of GBP 653,000. Overspends were recorded on several lines linked to outputs that met or exceeded targets, including OP1.1 at GBP 174,850 against GBP 162,000, OP2.1 at GBP 148,900 against GBP 121,000, OP3.1 at GBP 151,440 against GBP 146,000, OP3.2 at GBP 109,250 against GBP 103,000, and OP4.3 at GBP 58,630 against GBP 54,000. Some lines underspent: OP1.3 spent GBP 81,330 against GBP 88,000; OP2.2 spent GBP 39,600 against GBP 42,000; OP3.3 spent GBP 24,980 against GBP 31,000; and OP4.1 spent GBP 32,700 against GBP 39,000.

The available evidence suggests that overspend did not reflect weak control alone; in several cases it sat alongside over-delivery on outputs. However, one financial management issue remained unresolved in the review period: partner returns used a review window of 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25 while the award letter set the first Annual Review period as 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025. Finance had not yet recut to the FCDO review window at the point of reporting, so comparability between delivery and financial reporting periods was not fully aligned.

No evidence suggested funds were used other than as intended. Hardship grant controls included deduplication of caregiver records before payment, and submitted information reported no new material risks beyond those already captured in the grant risk register. Commercial performance could only be assessed in limited terms from the submitted record: no supplier or consultant performance issues were reported in the evidence provided for this section.

On management actions and compliance with FCDO processes, the programme maintained documented district learning meetings and prepared for the review pack due under the award letter requirements. Follow-up actions were clearly identified: recut finance to the FCDO review window; chase late Term 3 attendance registers from four schools; complete menstrual health training in the three remaining schools; and finish disposal bins linked to four latrine units.

content.text:
Recommendations from the current review focused on three corrective actions. First, the team identified the need to recut finance to the FCDO review window of 15 October to 14 October, as partner returns were still using 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25 and finance had not yet been recut. Second, the review highlighted the need to complete menstrual health training in the three remaining schools, linked to OP2.2 performance of 17 schools reached against a target of 20. Third, the review called for submission of late attendance registers, as four schools submitted registers late and this affected OP1.2 reporting.

Updates on previous recommendations showed partial progress. Earlier actions on register cleaning were partly completed, and September deduplication removed double-count risk on OP1.1. This was consistent with district validation samples that confirmed re-entry figures, while attendance reporting remained weaker because of late submissions from four schools.

Priorities for the next period were therefore clear and evidence-based. The programme needed to close the OP2.2 gap from 17 of 20 schools, complete disposal bins at four latrine units, and align reporting period labelling with the award letter. These actions responded directly to Year 1 delivery issues rather than new material risks: no new material risks were reported beyond those already in the grant risk register.
assumptions: Exact due dates for each action were not available in submitted records, except that one action plan item stated completion by Q1 next period.
Priority levels and implementation status labels for each recommendation were not explicitly provided in the source records and are therefore not assigned.
The required recommendations action plan table could not be fully populated with dated rows because submitted records did not provide complete due dates or status fields for each action.

content.text:
Annual Review 1 covered the formal period from 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025 under FCDO grant MWI-EDU-AR-4471. The programme remained broadly on track against Year 1 milestones, with delivery concentrated on girls’ re-enrolment, attendance support, school WASH access, hardship support and district learning processes.

Headline output results were mixed but generally positive. OP1.1 exceeded its Year 1 milestone: 684 out-of-school or at-risk girls were re-enrolled or newly retained against a target of 650. OP1.2 reached 472 supported girls attending at least 80% of school days against a target of 500, so performance was slightly below plan. OP1.3 also exceeded its milestone, reaching 438 girls completing at least 20 remedial learning sessions against a target of 420. In the school environment and protection area, OP2.1 delivered 31 separate lockable girls’ latrine stances against a target of 24, while OP2.2 reached 17 schools with menstrual health supplies and trained focal teachers against a target of 20. On household support, OP3.1 reached 392 caregivers with an education hardship grant against a target of 400, OP3.2 reached 571 girls with a school re-entry kit or learning materials package against a target of 550, and OP3.3 recorded follow-up for hardship grant households at 0.68 against a milestone of 0.75. Systems and learning outputs were also largely delivered: three district learning meetings were held against a target of four, and 136 school or community actors were trained on girls’ re-entry and safeguarding protocols against a target of 120.

Available outcome evidence indicated improvement in attendance and retention during the review period. Monitoring used term attendance registers and school safeguarding pathway checks, and submitted records stated that supported girls’ attendance and retention improved against Year 1 milestones, with variance notes captured in the AR1 export.

The main issues were operational rather than strategic. Menstrual health supply delays affected OP2.2, which remained at 17 of 20 schools by period end. Three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training, which affected completion in that area. Four schools submitted attendance registers late, which weakened the completeness of OP1.2 reporting. There was also a reporting alignment issue: partner returns used the period 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25 while the award letter set the Annual Review period as 15-Oct-24 to 14-Oct-25, and finance had not yet recut figures to that formal window.

Risk remained manageable based on available evidence. No new material risks beyond those already in the grant risk register were reported. Safeguarding referral pathways were tested in supported schools, with no major incident trend reported in Year 1 monitoring returns. There was no evidence that funds were used other than as intended; hardship grant controls removed duplicate risk by deduplicating 16 caregiver records before payment.

Financially, the AR1 export showed total output-line budget of GBP 880,000 against actual spend of GBP 920,420 for the review period presented in that file, indicating overspend against those lines overall. Variance was visible across outputs: for example, OP1.1 spent more than budgeted, while OP4.1 spent less than budgeted. Because submitted partner returns used a different review-period labelling from the award letter window, these figures should be read alongside that limitation.

Agreed follow-up actions were clear: recut finance to the FCDO review window of 15 October to 14 October; secure late attendance registers from four schools; complete menstrual health training in the remaining three schools; and finish disposal bins at four latrine units.
