content.text:
Delivery against the outcome objective, “Girls demonstrate improved retention, attendance and learning continuity,” remained broadly on track during Year 1. Monitoring drew on term attendance registers and school safeguarding pathway checks, and the Annual Review export recorded variance notes against indicator lines. Performance was strongest on re-enrolment, school WASH access, remedial learning participation, hardship grant delivery, re-entry kits, and training of school and community actors.

Against expected results, OP1.1 exceeded its Year 1 milestone: 684 girls were re-enrolled or newly retained against a target of 650. OP2.1 also exceeded plan, with 31 separate lockable girls’ latrine stances rehabilitated or made newly functional against a target of 24. OP1.3 reached 438 girls completing at least 20 remedial learning sessions against a target of 420. OP3.1 was close to target at 392 caregivers receiving an education hardship grant against a target of 400, while OP3.2 slightly exceeded plan with 571 girls receiving a school re-entry kit or learning materials package against a target of 550. OP4.3 also exceeded its Year 1 milestone, with 136 school or community actors trained on girls’ re-entry and safeguarding protocols against a target of 120.

A smaller number of indicators fell below milestone. OP1.2 reached 472 supported girls attending at least 80% of school days against a target of 500. Available evidence indicates that four schools submitted attendance registers late, which affected reporting for this line. OP2.2 reached 17 schools with menstrual health supplies and trained focal teachers against a target of 20. Records attribute this shortfall to menstrual health supply delays, and the assumption that focal teachers would be available held in most schools but not fully: three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training. OP3.3 also underperformed against milestone, with verified attendance follow-up within 45 days recorded at 0.68 against a target of 0.75.

These results suggest that the programme made credible early progress toward improved retention and attendance for supported girls, but performance was uneven across the package of support needed to sustain those gains. Re-enrolment delivery was ahead of plan, and district validation samples confirmed re-entry figures. Attendance improvement was positive but weaker than the re-enrolment result, which is consistent with late register submission affecting completeness of reporting and with some support components still incomplete in a small number of schools.

The evidence base was adequate for an Annual Review judgement, though not without limitations. Evidence included school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists, and district validation samples. No standalone external evaluation was commissioned in Year 1; monitoring relied on termly indicator returns and partner spot checks. Data quality constraints remained material in two areas: first, partner returns used a review period of 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25 while the award letter cited 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025; second, late submission of attendance registers from four schools affected completeness for OP1.2.

Risk conditions remained stable overall. No new material risks were reported beyond those already in the grant risk register. No major climate shock stopped delivery in Year 1, although lake-shore transport costs increased for OP1.1 activities. Safeguarding referral pathways were tested in supported schools, and no major incident trend was reported through Year 1 monitoring returns.

Overall conclusion: programme delivery achieved solid first-year progress against the outcome pathway and most measured output milestones were met or exceeded. The main deviations were concentrated in attendance reporting completeness, menstrual health implementation in three remaining schools within the Year 1 target set, and follow-up verification for hardship grant households. The clearest lesson from the period was that strong front-end delivery on re-enrolment needed equally consistent school-level reporting and completion of supporting services to translate into stronger attendance performance.

On Output 1, OP1.1 exceeded its AR1 milestone: 684 girls were re-enrolled or newly retained against a milestone of 650. OP1.3 also exceeded plan, with 438 girls completing at least 20 remedial learning sessions against a milestone of 420. OP1.2 fell slightly short, reaching 472 supported girls attending at least 80% of school days against a milestone of 500. The main reporting constraint was data completeness rather than evidence of non-delivery: four schools submitted attendance registers late, which affected OP1.2 reporting. District validation samples confirmed the re-entry figures, and previous register-cleaning actions were partly completed, with September deduplication removing double-count risk on OP1.1.

On Output 2, OP2.1 performed above milestone, delivering 31 separate lockable girls' latrine stances against a target of 24. OP2.2 reached 17 schools with menstrual health supplies and trained focal teachers against a milestone of 20. The shortfall was linked to menstrual health supply delays, and the assumption that focal teachers would be available held in most schools but not all: three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training. No new material risks beyond those already captured in the grant risk register were reported.

On Output 3, available indicators showed mixed but generally close-to-plan delivery. OP3.1 reached 392 caregivers with an education hardship grant against a milestone of 400. OP3.2 slightly exceeded milestone, reaching 571 girls with a school re-entry kit or learning materials package against a target of 550. OP3.3 reached 0.68 against an AR1 milestone of 0.75 for verified attendance follow-up within 45 days among hardship grant households. Monitoring records also noted that hardship grant records were deduplicated for 16 caregivers before payment, and no evidence was found that funds were used other than as intended.

On Output 4, OP4.3 exceeded its AR1 milestone: 136 school or community actors were trained on girls' re-entry and safeguarding protocols against a target of 120. OP4.1 was slightly below plan, with 3 district learning meetings held against a milestone of 4, though these meetings had documented action points and fed into district review processes.

The evidence base for output scoring relied on school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists, district validation samples, termly indicator returns and partner spot checks. Data quality was adequate for Annual Review scoring, but one issue remained material for interpretation: partner returns used the period 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25 while the award letter defined Annual Review coverage as 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025, and finance had not yet recut to that window.

Required output score values on the FCDO five-point scale were not supplied in numeric form in the submitted facts set. However, the available evidence supported higher scoring for outputs that met or exceeded AR1 milestones and lower scoring where milestones were missed or reporting remained incomplete.

content.text:
Monitoring during Year 1 relied on routine programme data rather than a standalone external evaluation. Submitted records stated that outcome monitoring used term attendance registers and school safeguarding pathway checks, while wider monitoring relied on termly indicator returns and partner spot checks. Indicator actuals were drawn from the BridgeLight AR1 export, with source notes per output, and the evidence base included school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists, and district validation samples.

On that basis, the evidence was adequate to support a cautious assessment of output delivery. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures, and attendance and financial lines included variance explanations in the AR1 export. The records supported several reported Year 1 results against milestone targets: OP1.1 reached 684 girls re-enrolled against a target of 650; OP1.2 reached 472 girls attending at least 80% of school days against a target of 500; OP2.1 delivered 31 separate lockable girls latrine stances against a target of 24; OP3.1 reached 392 caregivers receiving an education hardship grant against a target of 400; OP3.2 reached 571 girls receiving a school re-entry kit or learning materials package against a target of 550; OP3.3 recorded follow-up for hardship grant households at 0.68 against a milestone of 0.75; OP4.1 held 3 district learning meetings against a target of 4; and OP4.3 trained 136 school or community actors against a target of 120.

The submitted evidence also showed where performance fell short and why confidence should be moderated. No standalone external evaluation was commissioned in Year 1, so findings depended on routine monitoring systems and partner verification rather than independent assessment. Four schools submitted attendance registers late, which affected OP1.2 reporting. In addition, the review period used in partner returns was recorded as 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25, while the award letter set the Annual Review period at 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025; finance had not recut to that window at the point of reporting. This meant the evidence base was usable, but not fully aligned across narrative, indicator timing and finance.

New evidence generated during the year strengthened verification for infrastructure and transfer-related outputs. WASH engineer certificates supported reporting on sanitation works, including the record that OP2.1 achieved 31 latrine stances in Year 1. Mobile-money hardship grant lists provided an auditable trail for cash transfers linked to attendance plans, while district validation samples checked reported re-entry figures before consolidation. Submitted records also noted that September deduplication removed double-count risk on OP1.1, which improved confidence in the reported re-enrolment figure.

Evaluation findings remained limited in scope because no separate evaluation product was produced during the year. That conclusion should be read as provisional rather than independently tested. The strongest evidence sat around directly countable outputs with documentary traces; confidence was lower where data depended on late school register submission or where reporting windows were inconsistent.

content.text:
No new material risks were reported beyond those already recorded in the grant risk register during the review period. Delivery remained broadly on track, but two implementation issues affected performance and required active management. First, menstrual health supply delays contributed to OP2.2 reaching 17 schools against an AR1 milestone target of 20. Second, lake-shore transport costs increased for OP1.1, although no major climate shock stopped delivery in Year 1.

The programme managed these issues through routine monitoring and follow-up rather than through a reset of the overall risk profile. The assumption that community focal teachers would be available held in most schools, but three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training. That constraint helps explain the shortfall on OP2.2 alongside the reported supply delays. Attendance reporting also faced a data-quality issue: four schools submitted registers late, which affected OP1.2 reporting and limited timely verification for that indicator.

Safeguarding controls remained in place during the period. Safeguarding referral pathways were tested in supported schools, and Year 1 monitoring returns did not show any major incident trend. Outcome monitoring also used school safeguarding pathway checks alongside term attendance registers, which provided an additional control on whether supported girls were being reached in safer learning environments.

Financial control arrangements identified no evidence that funds were used other than as intended. For hardship grants, 16 caregiver records were deduplicated before payment, which reduced the risk of duplicate transfer and showed that payment controls were applied before disbursement. Evidence available for verification included school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists, and district validation samples.

There was one cross-cutting control issue in the reporting architecture rather than delivery itself. Partner returns used a review period of 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25, while the award letter set the Annual Review period at 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025; finance had not yet recut to that window. This did not indicate misuse of funds, but it did reduce precision in period matching for some reported results and expenditure lines and should be treated as a reporting control issue.

Overall, risk was managed within expected parameters during the period. Material safeguarding concerns did not increase, no misuse of funds was identified, and operational variances were specific and traceable: supply delays affected OP2.2; missing female focal teachers constrained training in three schools; late registers from four schools affected attendance reporting; and transport cost pressure increased on lake-shore delivery routes.

content.text:
Value for Money was assessed against economy, efficiency, effectiveness and equity using the AR1 finance export, indicator actuals and Year 1 monitoring evidence. The AR1 output budget totalled 880000, against actual spend of 920420. This represented an overspend of 40420 across the AR1 output lines and means cost control was mixed rather than uniform across outputs.

Economy. Spending pressure was concentrated in a small number of lines. OP1.1 spent 174850 against a budget of 162000, OP1.2 spent 98740 against 94000, OP2.1 spent 148900 against 121000, OP3.1 spent 151440 against 146000, OP3.2 spent 109250 against 103000, and OP4.3 spent 58630 against 54000. Other lines came in below budget: OP1.3 spent 81330 against 88000, OP2.2 spent 39600 against 42000, OP3.3 spent 24980 against 31000, and OP4.1 spent 32700 against 39000. Monitoring notes indicate that lake-shore transport costs increased for OP1.1, while menstrual health supply delays affected OP2.2. There was no evidence that funds were used other than intended; hardship grant records were deduplicated before payment, removing duplicate caregiver entries from the payment list.

Efficiency. Delivery remained broadly on track despite these cost pressures. Several outputs met or exceeded their AR1 milestones: OP1.1 reached 684 girls re-enrolled or newly retained against a milestone of 650; OP1.3 reached 438 girls completing remedial sessions against 420; OP2.1 delivered 31 latrine stances against 24; OP3.1 reached 392 caregivers receiving hardship grants against 400; OP3.2 reached 571 girls receiving re-entry kits or learning materials against 550; and OP4.3 reached 136 actors trained against 120. Two areas fell short: OP1.2 recorded 472 girls attending at least eighty percent of school days against a milestone of 500, and OP2.2 reached 17 schools with menstrual health supplies and trained focal teachers against a milestone of 20. The attendance shortfall was linked to late register submission from four schools rather than a reported delivery stop, while the OP2.2 gap reflected supply delays and the absence of a female focal teacher in three schools.

Effectiveness. Results suggest that spending translated into substantive output delivery in most areas tied to the programme outcome that girls demonstrate improved retention, attendance and learning continuity. Outcome monitoring used term attendance registers and school safeguarding pathway checks, and Year 1 reporting stated that supported girls' attendance and retention improved against Year 1 milestones with variance notes recorded in the AR1 export. Evidence for achieved outputs included school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists and district validation samples. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures, which strengthens confidence that spending on access-related activities produced verified results.

Equity. Available evidence indicates that resources were directed toward girls facing barriers to re-entry and continuity in school through support packages, hardship grants, learning materials and menstrual health support. The programme also trained school and community actors on girls' re-entry and safeguarding protocols, reaching 136 people in AR1, and held three district learning meetings with documented action points. However, exact disaggregation by gender, age or vulnerability within these output totals was not available in the submitted records for this section, so equity assessment relied on the design of the supported outputs rather than full beneficiary breakdowns.

Forecast versus actual costs require caution in interpretation. One gap answer states that sampled Year 1 lines totalled actual spend of GBP 694860 against forecast GBP 653000, while the AR1 export shows total output spend of 920420 against budget of 880000 across all listed output lines. In addition, partner returns used a review period of 01-Oct-24 to thirty September twenty twenty-five while the award letter cites fifteen October twenty twenty-four to fourteen October twenty twenty-five, and finance had not recut the period at the time of reporting.

Overall, Value for Money was acceptable but uneven in Year one: effectiveness was stronger than economy; efficiency was sound on most outputs but weakened by reporting delays and some input bottlenecks; equity intent was evident but not fully quantified from available disaggregation.

sections.label: F. Programme Management: Delivery, Commercial and Financial Performance

content.text:
Delivery in Year 1 remained broadly on track, with partner performance strongest on re-enrolment and WASH infrastructure outputs and weaker where reporting timeliness or supply delays affected completion. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures, which supported reported delivery on OP1.1. The programme achieved 684 girls re-enrolled against the AR1 milestone target of 650, and delivered 31 separate lockable girls’ latrine stances against a target of 24. Attendance performance was slightly below plan at 472 girls attending at least 80% of school days against a target of 500. Late register submission from four schools affected attendance reporting and limited completeness of OP1.2 data during the review period.

Financial delivery exceeded the AR1 output budget recorded in the export. Total AR1 actual spend was 920420 against an AR1 budget of 880000. At output level, overspend was recorded on OP1.1, OP1.2, OP2.1, OP3.1, OP3.2 and OP4.3, while underspend was recorded on OP1.3, OP2.2, OP3.3 and OP4.1. The largest positive variances were on OP2.1, where actual spend was 148900 against a budget of 121000, and on OP1.1, where actual spend was 174850 against a budget of 162000. Available management evidence linked cost pressure on OP1.1 to increased lake-shore transport costs. By contrast, underspend on OP2.2 aligned with incomplete delivery: menstrual health supply delays meant the programme reached 17 schools against an AR1 milestone target of 20.

Commercial and procurement issues were limited in the submitted record, but implementation did face operational delays linked to menstrual health supplies and to staffing assumptions in some schools. The assumption that community focal teachers would be available held in most schools; however, three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training. Safeguarding referral pathways were tested in supported schools, and no major incident trend was reported in Year 1 monitoring returns. There was also no evidence that funds were used other than as intended; hardship grant records were deduplicated before payment, removing duplicate-payment risk in 16 caregiver records.

Management attention is still required on reporting accuracy and period alignment. The award letter set the Annual Review period as 2024-10-15 to 2025-10-14, but partner returns used 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25 and finance had not recut the figures to the FCDO review window at the time of reporting. That affects comparability between narrative delivery reporting and financial presentation more than it affects whether activities took place, but it remains a control issue for the next submission cycle.

FCDO management requirements for this review cycle were clear in the award documentation: an Annual Review narrative, updated logframe, Value for Money assessment, forecast versus actual expenditure statement, risk and safeguarding update, any evaluation or learning outputs produced during the year, and recommendations with an action plan were required for the pack due by 2025-11-21. Delivery systems generated supporting evidence through school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists and district validation samples; no standalone external evaluation was commissioned in Year 1.

Overall, programme management delivered most Year 1 outputs with evidence of routine verification and district-level follow-up meetings. The main management issues were overspend against AR1 budget lines, delayed menstrual health inputs affecting OP2.2 completion, late school registers affecting attendance reporting, and unresolved alignment between partner reporting dates and the formal FCDO Annual Review period.

content.text:
Current review recommendations were driven by three issues recorded during Year 1. First, the programme needed to recut finance and reporting to the FCDO Annual Review window of 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025, because partner returns used 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25 and finance had not yet been recut. Second, implementation follow-up was required on menstrual health delivery: OP2.2 reached 17 schools against an AR1 milestone of 20, and submitted records linked the shortfall to menstrual health supply delays and the absence of a female focal teacher in three schools. Third, attendance reporting needed corrective action because four schools submitted registers late, which affected OP1.2 reporting.

Updates on previous recommendations were mixed. Earlier actions on register cleaning were only partially complete, but September deduplication removed double-count risk on OP1.1. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures, which gave reasonable assurance on that result line, while attendance data remained weaker because of the late school submissions.

The action plan for the next period was therefore kept focused and practical: recut the AR1 period to match the award letter; chase and secure the missing Term 3 attendance registers; and complete the remaining menstrual health actions, including training in the three schools still without a female focal teacher and finishing disposal bins linked to four latrine units.

Recommendations and action points:
- Recommendation: Recut finance and reporting period labelling to match the FCDO review window. Owner: Programme Manager. Due date: exact due date was not available in submitted records; records only stated Q1 next period. Priority: High. Status: Open. Follow-up required: confirm revised AR1 pack uses the award-letter review period.
- Recommendation: Obtain late attendance registers from four schools and close OP1.2 reporting gaps. Owner: M&E. Due date: exact due date was not available in submitted records. Priority: High. Status: Open. Follow-up required: verify updated attendance figures once Term 3 registers are received.
- Recommendation: Complete menstrual health training in the three remaining schools and close the OP2.2 gap from 17 to 20 schools. Owner: WASH. Due date: exact due date was not available in submitted records. Priority: High. Status: Open. Follow-up required: confirm trained focal teachers are in place and supplies are delivered.
- Recommendation: Finish disposal bins at four latrine units. Owner: WASH. Due date: exact due date was not available in submitted records. Priority: Medium. Status: Open. Follow-up required: verify completion through implementation records.

The first Annual Review covered 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025, with the review pack due by 21 November 2025 [fact:reporting_period_ar1.start; fact:reporting_period_ar1.end; fact:reporting_deadline.annual_review_pack]. The programme reference was MWI-EDU-AR-4471 and the total approved FCDO contribution was GBP 1,240,000 across the full programme period from 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2026 [fact:grant_reference; fact:award_budget.amount; fact:grant_period.start; fact:grant_period.end]. Year 1 delivery remained broadly on track [gap:summary_and_overview:indicator:overall_progress].

Results were mixed but generally positive against Year 1 targets. Under Output 1, OP1.1 exceeded target, reaching 684 against 650, while OP1.3 also exceeded target at 438 against 420 [fact:indicators.OP1.1.actual; fact:indicators.OP1.1.target; fact:indicators.OP1.3.actual; fact:indicators.OP1.3.target]. OP1.2 fell short, with attendance at 80%+ recorded at 472 against a target of 500 [fact:indicators.OP1.2.actual; fact:indicators.OP1.2.target]. Submitted records explained that four schools sent attendance registers late, which affected OP1.2 reporting [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations].

Under Output 2, OP2.1 surpassed target, delivering 31 latrine stances against 24 [fact:indicators.OP2.1.actual; fact:indicators.OP2.1.target]. OP2.2 reached 17 schools against a target of 20 [fact:indicators.OP2.2.actual; fact:indicators.OP2.2.target]. Records attributed this shortfall to menstrual health supply delays, and noted that three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:new_risks; gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:realised_assumptions].

Under Output 3, hardship grant support and learning materials were delivered close to or above plan in two areas but follow-up lagged behind target. OP3.1 reached 392 against a target of 400, while OP3.2 exceeded target at 571 against 550 [fact:indicators.OP3.1.actual; fact:indicators.OP3.1.target; fact:indicators.OP3.2.actual; fact:indicators.OP3.2.target]. Verified attendance follow-up within 45 days reached 0.68 against a target of 0.75 for OP3.3 [fact:indicators.OP3.3.actual; fact:indicators.OP3.3.target]. Under Output 4, district learning meetings reached 3 against a target of 4 for OP4.1, while training on girls' re-entry and safeguarding protocols exceeded plan at 136 against a target of 120 for OP4.3 [fact:indicators.OP4.1.actual; fact:indicators.OP4.1.target; fact:indicators.OP4.3.actual; fact:indicators.OP4.3.target].

Financial delivery ran above the Year 1 budget envelope in the AR1 export, with total actual spend of GBP 920,420 against a Year 1 budget of GBP 880,000 [fact:financials.lines.TOTAL.actual; fact:financials.lines.TOTAL.budget]. Overspends were recorded on several lines that also showed strong delivery, including OP1.1 at GBP 174,850 against GBP 162,000, OP2.1 at GBP 148,900 against GBP 121,000, and OP4.3 at GBP b58,630 נגד GBP b54,000? content.text:
Delivery against expected results was mixed but broadly positive during the first Annual Review period from 2024-10-15 to 2025-10-14. Outcome monitoring used term attendance registers and school safeguarding pathway checks, and reported improvements in supported girls' attendance and retention against Year 1 milestones, with variance notes recorded in the AR1 export [gap:performance_and_conclusions:table:outcome_assessment].

Performance at output level showed several areas ahead of target. Under OP1, re-enrolment or new retention reached 684 against a target of 650, while completion of at least 20 remedial learning sessions reached 438 against a target of 420 [fact:indicators.OP1.1.actual, fact:indicators.OP1.1.target, fact:indicators.OP1.3.actual, fact:indicators.OP1.3.target]. Attendance at 80% or more of school days reached 472 against a target of 500, so this result remained below plan [fact:indicators.OP1.2.actual, fact:indicators.OP1.2.target]. Submitted evidence indicates that four schools sent attendance registers late, which affected OP1.2 reporting [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations]. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures, and September deduplication removed double-count risk on OP1.1, which strengthened confidence in the re-enrolment result [gap:programme_management_delivery_commercial_financial:indicator:partner_performance, gap:recommendations_and_actions:indicator:updates_on_previous_recommendations].

Under OP2, delivery was uneven. Girls' latrine stances rehabilitated or newly functional reached 31 against a target of 24, exceeding the Year 1 milestone [fact:indicators.OP2.1.actual, fact:indicators.OP2.1.target]. By contrast, schools with menstrual health supplies and trained focal teachers reached 17 against a target of 20 [fact:indicators.OP2.2.actual, fact:indicators.OP2.2.target]. The reported reason was delay in menstrual health supplies; this was treated as an implementation constraint rather than a new material risk [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:new_risks]. A related assumption held in most schools, but three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training, which helps explain the shortfall [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:realised_assumptions].

Under OP3, hardship support and learning materials were delivered close to or above plan on two measures but follow-up lagged. Caregivers receiving an education hardship grant reached 392 against a target of 400 [fact:indicators.OP3.1.actual, fact:indicators.OP3.1.target]. Girls receiving a school re-entry kit or learning materials package reached 571 against a target of 550 [fact:indicators.OP3.2.actual, fact:indicators.OP3.2.target]. Verified attendance follow-up within 45 days reached 0.68 against a target of 0.75 [fact:indicators.OP3.3.actual, fact:indicators.OP3.3.target]. Monitoring records also stated that there was no evidence of funds not used as intended; hardship grants deduplicated 16 caregiver records before payment [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:funds_not_used_as_intended_risk]. That check reduced payment risk even though follow-up timeliness stayed below target.

Under OP4, district coordination and training results were again mixed. District learning meetings with documented action points reached 3 against a target of 4 [fact:indicators.OP4.1.actual, fact:indicators.OP4.1.target]. School and community actors trained on girls' re-entry and safeguarding protocols reached 136 against a target of 120 [fact:indicators.OP4.3.actual, fact:indicators.OP4.3.target]. Safeguarding referral pathways were tested in supported schools, and no major incident trend was reported in Year 1 monitoring returns [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:safeguarding_risk_where_relevant]. This suggests that safeguarding systems were functioning at an operational level even where some activity milestones were not fully met.

Financial delivery ran above the Year 1 budget shown in the AR1 export. Total actual spend was GBP 920420 against a Year 1 budget of GBP 880000 [fact:financials.lines.TOTAL.actual, fact:financials.lines.TOTAL.budget]. Overspend appeared in several lines that also met or exceeded targets, including OP1.1 at GBP 174850 against GBP 162000, OP2.1 at GBP 148900 against GBP 121000, OP3.2 at GBP 109250 against GBP 103000, and OP4.3 at GBP 58630 against GBP 54000 [fact:financials.lines.OP1.1.actual, fact:financials.lines.OP1.1.budget, fact:financials.lines.OP2.1.actual, fact:financials.lines.OP2.1.budget, fact:financials.lines.OP3.2.actual, fact:financials.lines.OP3.2.budget, fact:financials.lines.OP4..actual??]

content.text:
Output scoring for Annual Review 1 was drawn from the BridgeLight AR1 export, which populated proposed scores and variance explanations at indicator level. Performance was broadly on track, with stronger delivery on several access, WASH and material support indicators, and shortfalls concentrated in attendance reporting, menstrual health coverage, follow-up timeliness and district learning meetings [gap:detailed_output_scoring:indicator:output_scores][fact:reporting_period_ar1.start][fact:reporting_period_ar1.end].

Under Output 1, re-enrolment or retention exceeded target at 684 against 650, while remedial learning completion also exceeded target at 438 against 420. Attendance at 80% or above reached 472 against a target of 500. The attendance variance reflected late register submission from four schools, which affected reporting completeness during the review period rather than indicating wider delivery failure in re-entry support [fact:indicators.OP1.1.actual][fact:indicators.OP1.1.target][fact:indicators.OP1.3.actual][fact:indicators.OP1.3.target][fact:indicators.OP1.2.actual][fact:indicators.OP1.2.target][gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations].

Under Output 2, latrine rehabilitation outperformed plan at 31 against a target of 24. By contrast, schools with menstrual health supplies and trained focal teachers reached 17 against a target of 20. Reported variance was linked to menstrual health supply delays, and the assumption that focal teachers would be available held in most schools but not all; three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training [fact:indicators.OP2.1.actual][fact:indicators.OP2.1.target][fact:indicators.OP2.2.actual][fact:indicators.OP2.2.target][gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:new_risks][gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:realised_assumptions].

Under Output 3, hardship grant delivery was close to plan at 392 against a target of 400, and learning materials distribution exceeded target at 571 against 550. The weaker result sat in verified attendance follow-up within 45 days, which reached 0.68 against a target of 0.75. Even so, controls over transfer delivery appear to have held: no evidence was reported of funds not used as intended, and hardship grant processing deduplicated 16 caregiver records before payment [fact:indicators.OP3.1.actual][fact:indicators.OP3.1.target][fact:indicators.OP3.2.actual][fact:indicators.OP3.2.target][fact:indicators.OP3.3.actual][fact:indicators.OP3.3.target][gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:funds_not_used_as_intended_risk].

Under Output 4, district learning meetings reached 3 against a target of 4, while school and community actors trained on girls' re-entry and safeguarding protocols exceeded target at 136 against 120 [fact:indicators.OP4.1.actual][fact:indicators.OP4.1.target][fact:indicators.OP4.3.actual][fact:indicators.OP4.3.target]. Safeguarding referral pathways were tested in supported schools, and Year 1 monitoring returns did not report any major incident trend [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:safeguarding_risk_where_relevant].

Evidence for scoring came from school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists and district validation samples. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures; however, the evidence base had two limits that matter for score interpretation. First, partner returns used a review window of 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25 while the award letter set Annual Review 1 as 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025; finance had not yet recut to the formal FCDO window. Second, some attendance documentation arrived late [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:new_evidence][gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations][fact:funder][fact:funder_display_name].

The output scores should therefore be read as reasonable Annual Review judgements based on available evidence rather than as fully recut results to the formal reporting dates.

content.text:
Monitoring in Year 1 relied on the programme logframe and routine partner reporting rather than a standalone external evaluation. Indicator actuals were drawn from the BridgeLight AR1 export, with source notes recorded per output, and attendance and financial lines included variance explanations. Monitoring data was supported by school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists, and district validation samples. No standalone external evaluation was commissioned in Year 1; monitoring instead used termly indicator returns and partner spot checks. [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:evidence_base_strength] [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:new_evidence] [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:evaluation_progress]

The submitted records gave a usable evidence base for reviewing output delivery, but the strength of evidence varied by result area. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures, which supported reported progress on OP1.1, where actual achievement reached 684 against a target of 650. Attendance evidence was weaker because four schools submitted registers late, which affected OP1.2 reporting; this helps explain why attendance at 80% or above reached 472 against a target of 500 and should be read with some caution. For infrastructure and material support outputs, the evidence trail was more direct: OP2.1 reported 31 against a target of 24, OP3.1 reported 392 against a target of 400, and OP3.2 reported 571 against a target of 550. [gap:programme_management_delivery_commercial_financial:indicator:partner_performance] [fact:indicators.OP1.1.actual] [fact:indicators.OP1.1.target] [fact:indicators.OP1.2.actual] [fact:indicators.OP1.2.target] [fact:indicators.OP2.1.actual] [fact:indicators.OP2.1.target] [fact:indicators.OP3.1.actual] [fact:indicators.OP3.1.target] [fact:indicators.OP3.2.actual] [fact:indicators.OP3.2.target]

Evidence limitations affected both period alignment and completeness. Partner returns used a review window of 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25, while the formal Annual Review period in the award letter ran from 2024-10-15 to 2025-10-14, and finance had not recut to that formal window at the time of reporting. This did not invalidate the Year 1 picture, but it reduced precision when matching programme records to the FCDO review period and means some figures should be treated as management-reporting figures aligned to partner returns rather than fully recast Annual Review figures. [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations] [fact:reporting_period_ar1.start] [fact:reporting_period_ar1.end]

The main variance that appeared most clearly linked to evidence constraints was OP1.2 attendance reporting, where late register submission weakened completeness of the dataset. A second issue sat partly with delivery and partly with evidence timing under OP2.2: menstrual health supply delays affected performance, with actual achievement at 17 against a target of 20 schools. The records therefore supported a cautious conclusion that Year 1 delivery remained broadly on track overall, while some output areas were assessed on stronger administrative evidence than others. [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:new_risks] [fact:indicators.OP2.2.actual] [fact:indicators.OP2.2.target] [gap:summary_and_overview:indicator:overall_progress]

Outcome monitoring used term attendance registers and school safeguarding pathway checks, and submitted records indicated that supported girls' attendance and retention improved against Year 1 milestones, with variance notes recorded in the AR1 export. However, exact milestone values and any disaggregation by gender, age or vulnerability group were not available in the submitted records used for this section, so this assessment remained directional rather than fully independently verified at outcome level. That limitation matters because FCDO requires monitoring data to be disaggregated where relevant by gender, age and vulnerability group; the obligation was clear even though those breakdowns were not available here for review narrative purposes. [gap:performance_and_conclusions:table:outcome_assessment] [fact:reporting_obligations.data_disaggregation]

Overall, the Year 1 evidence base was adequate for an Annual Review judgement on outputs and spending trends, especially where documentary records could be checked against administrative sources such as registers, certificates and payment lists. It was less strong for exact period alignment and for attendance completeness in a small number of schools. On that basis, findings on over-target outputs were reasonably supported by submitted records, while under-target or near-target indicators should be interpreted alongside the stated data quality limits rather than as simple delivery failure alone. [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:evidence_base_strength] [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:new_evidence] [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations]

content.text:
No new material risks were reported beyond those already captured in the grant risk register. The main delivery issue during the period was delay in menstrual health supplies, which affected OP2.2 and left delivery at 17 schools against a target of 20. This was a contained implementation risk rather than a wider control failure, and it sat alongside stronger performance in related infrastructure delivery, where OP2.1 reached 31 latrine stances against a target of 24. [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:new_risks] [fact:indicators.OP2.2.actual] [fact:indicators.OP2.2.target] [fact:indicators.OP2.1.actual] [fact:indicators.OP2.1.target]

A key operating assumption held in most schools: focal teachers were available to support delivery. However, that assumption did not hold everywhere. Three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training, which helps explain the shortfall on OP2.2. The programme responded through routine implementation follow-up, but submitted records did not provide a formal revised risk rating for this issue. [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:realised_assumptions] [fact:indicators.OP2.2.actual] [fact:indicators.OP2.2.target]

Financial control arrangements remained in place during the review period. No evidence was reported that funds were used other than as intended, and hardship grant controls identified and removed duplicate entries before payment to reduce double-count risk. This was consistent with the wider evidence base retained for review, including payment records among the supporting documents that FCDO may request. [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:funds_not_used_as_intended_risk] [fact:reporting_obligations.supporting_documents]

Climate and environmental conditions created some cost pressure but did not stop delivery in Year 1. Lake-shore transport costs increased for OP1.1, and actual spend on that line reached GBP 174,850 against a budget of GBP 162,000. Even with that pressure, OP1.1 exceeded target performance, reaching 684 girls against a target of 650. No major climate shock was reported as having interrupted implementation during the year. [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:climate_environment_risk] [fact:financials.lines.OP1.1.actual] [fact:financials.lines.OP1.1.budget] [fact:indicators.OP1.1.actual] [fact:indicators.OP1.1.target]

Safeguarding controls remained active across supported schools. Referral pathways were tested during implementation, and Year 1 monitoring returns did not report any major incident trend. This does not remove safeguarding risk; it indicates that the programme continued to monitor referral functionality while no pattern of escalation was recorded in submitted returns during the period reviewed. [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:safeguarding_risk_where_relevant]

Overall, risk management during the first Annual Review period from 2024-10-15 to 2025-10-14 was stable, with operational issues identified and tracked through routine monitoring rather than through emergence of new material threats to delivery or fiduciary control. One data-related control issue remains relevant to assurance: partner returns used a different review window from the formal Annual Review period in the award letter, and finance had not recut those records at the time of reporting. That issue affects comparability and should be read alongside late attendance registers from four schools noted elsewhere in the evidence base, but it did not amount to reported misuse of funds or a major safeguarding deterioration during this review cycle. [fact:reporting_period_ar1.start] [fact:reporting_period_ar1.end] [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations]

content.text:
Value for Money in Year 1 was assessed against economy, efficiency, effectiveness and equity using the AR1 logframe and finance export, alongside monitoring evidence from school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists and district validation samples [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:evidence_base_strength; gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:new_evidence]. The formal first Annual Review period ran from 2024-10-15 to 2025-10-14, although partner returns used 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25 and finance had not recut the period at the time of reporting. That timing mismatch limited strict comparability for some Year 1 cost and results judgements [fact:reporting_period_ar1.start; fact:reporting_period_ar1.end; gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations].

Economy
Year 1 actual spend totalled GBP 920,420 against a Year 1 budget of GBP 880,000 across the AR1 output lines [fact:financials.lines.TOTAL.actual; fact:financials.lines.TOTAL.budget]. Variance was concentrated in several lines where delivery exceeded target or where input costs rose. OP1.1 spent GBP 174,850 against GBP 162,000 while reaching 684 against a target of 650 [fact:financials.lines.OP1.1.actual; fact:financials.lines.OP1.1.budget; fact:indicators.OP1.1.actual; fact:indicators.OP1.1.target]. The knowledge bank records that lake-shore transport costs increased for OP1.1, which helps explain higher unit cost on that line [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:climate_environment_risk]. OP2.1 spent GBP 148,900 against GBP 121,000 and delivered 31 latrine stances against a target of 24 [fact:financials.lines.OP2.1.actual; fact:financials.lines.OP2.1.budget; fact:indicators.OP2.1.actual; fact:indicators.OP2.1.target]. By contrast, some under-spend aligned with lower-than-target delivery or incomplete activity completion: OP2.2 spent GBP 39,600 against GBP 42,000 and reached 17 schools against a target of 20 [fact:financials.lines.OP2.2.actual; fact:financials.lines.OP2.2.budget; fact:indicators.OP2.2.actual; fact:indicators.OP2.2.target]. Menstrual health supply delays affected this line, and three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:new_risks; gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:realised_assumptions]. OP3.3 also underspent at GBP 24,980 against GBP 31,000 while follow-up reached 0.68 against a target of 0.75 [fact:financials.lines.OP3.3.actual; fact:financials.lines.OP3.3.budget; fact:indicators.OP3.3.actual; fact:indicators.OP3.3.target]. Overall, economy was mixed rather than weak: overspend was linked to delivery pressure and cost drivers that were visible in the records rather than unexplained budget drift [fact:financials.lines.TOTAL.actual; fact:financials.lines.TOTAL.budget].

Efficiency
Efficiency was strongest where spend translated into above-target output delivery. OP3.2 spent GBP 109,250 against GBP 103,000 and reached 571 girls against a target of 550 [fact:financials.lines.OP3.2.actual; fact:financials.lines.OP3.2.budget; fact:indicators.OP3.2.actual; fact:indicators.OP3.2.target]. OP4.3 spent GBP 58,630 against GBP 54,000 and trained 136 school or community actors against a target of 120 [fact:financials.lines.OP4.3.actual; fact:financials.lines.OP4.3.budget; fact:indicators.OP4.3.actual; fact:indicators.OP4.3.target]. OP1.3 showed the clearest efficiency gain in financial terms, with spend below budget at GBP 81,330 against GBP 88,000 while completions exceeded target at 438 against 420 [fact:financials.lines.OP1.3.actual; fact:financials.lines.OP1.3.budget; fact:indicators.OP1.3.actual; fact:indicators.OP1.X?]

content.text:
Delivery remained broadly on track during the first Annual Review period, with district validation samples confirming re-entry figures, although late register submission from four schools affected attendance reporting. Year 1 progress was mixed across outputs: OP1.1 reached 684 against a target of 650, OP2.1 reached 31 against 24, and OP4.3 reached 136 against 120. Other lines fell short or remained slightly below plan, including OP1.2 at 472 against 500, OP2.2 at 17 against 20, OP3.1 at 392 against 400, OP3.3 at 0.68 against 0.75, and OP4.1 at 3 against 4. The main reported delivery issue was menstrual health supply delays affecting OP2.2, alongside the absence of a female focal teacher in three schools for menstrual health training. No major climate shock stopped delivery in Year 1, although lake-shore transport costs increased for OP1.1.

Financial performance was above the Year 1 output budget recorded in the AR1 export. Total actual spend reached GBP 920,420 against a Year 1 budget of GBP 880,000. Overspends were recorded on several lines linked to stronger or accelerated delivery, including OP1.1 at GBP 174,850 against GBP 162,000, OP2.1 at GBP 148,900 against GBP 121,000, OP3.1 at GBP 151,440 against GBP 146,000, OP3.2 at GBP 109,250 against GBP 103,000, and OP4.3 at GBP 58,630 against GBP 54,000. Underspends were recorded where delivery lagged or some activities were incomplete, including OP2.2 at GBP 39,600 against GBP 42,000, OP3.3 at GBP 24,980 against GBP 31,000, and OP4.1 at GBP 32,700 against GBP 39,000.

There was also a reporting alignment issue between formal FCDO requirements and partner returns. The award letter set the first Annual Review period as 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025 and required the review pack by 21 November 2025. However, partner returns used the period from October to September and finance had not recut to the formal review window at the time of reporting. This limited full comparability between programme records and FCDO reporting dates.

On financial control and commercial assurance, no evidence was reported of funds not being used as intended; hardship grant records were deduplicated before payment for sixteen caregiver records. Evidence available for delivery and expenditure included school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists and district validation samples. Partner management actions focused on recutting the AR1 period to match the award letter window, obtaining late attendance registers from four schools and completing remaining menstrual health-related actions.

content.text:
Recommendations from the current review focused on closing the remaining delivery and reporting gaps identified in Year 1. The review recommended recutting finance to the formal FCDO Annual Review window of 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025, completing menstrual health training in the three remaining schools, and submitting the late attendance registers that affected attendance reporting. These actions were grounded in the evidence that partner returns used a different review period label, that OP2.2 reached 17 against a target of 20, and that four schools submitted attendance registers late. [gap:recommendations_and_actions:indicator:recommendations_from_current_review] [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations] [fact:indicators.OP2.2.actual] [fact:indicators.OP2.2.target] [fact:reporting_period_ar1.start] [fact:reporting_period_ar1.end]

Updates against previous recommendations showed partial progress. Earlier actions on register cleaning were partly completed, and September deduplication removed double-count risk on OP1.1. This was consistent with wider control findings that found no evidence of funds not used as intended, while hardship grant checks deduplicated 16 caregiver records before payment. [gap:recommendations_and_actions:indicator:updates_on_previous_recommendations] [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:funds_not_used_as_intended_risk]

Priorities carried into the next period were therefore tightly defined by unresolved Year 1 variance. The main operational priority was to close the OP2.2 gap at 17 out of 20 schools and complete disposal bins at four latrine units. A second priority was to align reporting period labelling with the award letter so that narrative, indicator and finance reporting matched the formal Annual Review period used by FCDO. [gap:recommendations_and_actions:indicator:priorities_for_next_period] [fact:indicators.OP2.2.actual] [fact:indicators.OP2.2.target]

The action plan recorded named owners for follow-up. The Programme Manager was assigned to recut the AR1 period by Q1 next period; M&E was assigned to chase the four schools for Term 3 registers; and WASH was assigned to finish disposal bins. Exact due dates beyond "Q1 next period" were not available in the submitted records, so the table records controlled follow-up rather than invented deadlines. [gap:recommendations_and_actions:table:recommendations_action_plan]

Status values for each action point were not explicitly provided in the source material, so table entries use evidence-based qualitative wording rather than unsupported completion claims.

This Annual Review covered the first review window set out in the award letter, from 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025, with the review pack due to FCDO by 21 November 2025. The programme reference was MWI-EDU-AR-4471, under the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office award of GBP 1,240,000. Submitted finance data for Year 1 recorded a budget allocation of GBP 880,000 and actual spend of GBP 920,420. Records also noted that partner returns used a different period label of 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25 and finance had not been recut at the point of review, which limited direct alignment between some delivery and financial reporting lines. Overall progress remained broadly on track in Year 1. Delivery exceeded target on several output indicators. The programme reached 684 girls re-enrolled or retained against a Year 1 target of 650. It reached 438 girls completing remedial sessions against a target of 420, delivered 31 functional girls' latrine stances against a target of 24, provided re-entry kits to 571 girls against a target of 550, and trained 136 school and community actors on re-entry and safeguarding against a target of 120. These results supported the stated objective that adolescent girls demonstrate improved school retention, attendance and learning continuity with reduced barriers. Outcome monitoring used term attendance registers and school safeguarding pathway checks, and submitted records stated that supported girls' attendance and retention improved against Year 1 milestones. Performance against the Outcome was positive overall, with Year 1 delivery broadly on track and most reported output milestones met or exceeded. The programme objective remained that adolescent girls demonstrate improved school retention, attendance and learning continuity with reduced barriers. Monitoring during the period used term attendance registers and school safeguarding pathway checks, and reported that supported girls’ attendance and retention improved against Year 1 milestones, with variance notes recorded in the AR1 export. [fact:objectives.out1_improved_retention_attendance;gap:performance_and_conclusions:table:outcome_assessment]

Reported output results showed stronger progress on re-enrolment, remedial support, re-entry support and training than on some system and attendance measures. Girls re-enrolled or retained reached 684 against a Year 1 target of 650. Girls completing remedial sessions reached 438 against a target of 420. Girls receiving re-entry kits reached 571 against a target of 550. School and community actors trained on re-entry and safeguarding reached 136 against a target of 120. Functional girls’ latrine stances reached 31 against a target of 24. These results indicated that direct support to girls and several enabling activities were delivered above plan during the reporting period. [fact:indicators.op1_1_girls_reenrolled_retained.y1_actual;fact:indicators.op1_1_girls_reenrolled_retained.y1_target;fact:indicators.op1_3_girls_remedial_sessions.y1_actual;fact:indicators.op1_3_girls_remedial_sessions.y1_target;fact:indicators.op3_2_girls_reentry_kit.y1_actual;fact:indicators.op3_2_girls_reentry_kit.y1_target;fact:indicators.op4_3_actors_trained_reentry.y1_actual;fact:indicators.op4_3_actors_trained_reentry.y1_target;fact:indicators.op2_1_latrine_stances_functional.y1_actual;fact:indicators.op2_1_latrine_stances_functional.y1_target]

A smaller set of indicators fell short of Year 1 targets. Girls attending at least 80% of school days reached 472 against a target of 500. Schools with menstrual health supplies and trained teachers reached 17 against a target of 20. Caregivers receiving hardship grants reached 392 against a target of 400. District learning meetings reached 3 against a target of 4. The proportion of hardship households with attendance follow-up was reported at 0.68 in Year 1, while the proposal set a Year 1 milestone of 75%. [fact:indicators.op1_2_girls_attending_80pct.y1_actual;fact:indicators.op1_2_girls_attending_80pct.y1_target;fact:indicators.op2_2_schools_menstrual_health.y1_actual;fact:indicators.op2_2_schools_menstrual_health.y1_target;fact:indicators.op3_1_caregivers_hardship_grant.y1_actual;fact:indicators.op3_1_caregivers_hardship_grant.y1_target;fact:indicators.op4_1_district_learning_meetings.y1_actual;fact:indicators.op4_1_district_learning_meetings.y1_target;fact:indicators.op3_3_hardship_households_followup.y1_actual]

The available evidence explained part of this variance. Four schools submitted attendance registers late, which affected OP1.2 reporting. Menstrual health supply delays affected OP2.2, and an assumption that community focal teachers would be available held in most schools but not fully, as three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training. These factors help explain why attendance and menstrual health indicators lagged behind stronger performance in re-enrolment, remedial delivery and infrastructure outputs. [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations;gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:new_risks;gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:realised_assumptions]

The evidence base was adequate for an Annual Review but had limits that should be kept in view when interpreting performance trends. Indicator actuals were drawn from the BridgeLight AR1 export with source notes per output, while evidence included school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists, and district validation samples. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures. At the same time, no standalone external evaluation was commissioned in Year 1, monitoring relied on termly indicator returns and partner spot checks, and partner returns used a review period of 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25 while the award letter cited the first Annual Review period as 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025. Finance had not recut to that window in the submitted material. Safeguarding and delivery controls appeared to function during the period based on submitted monitoring records. Safeguarding referral pathways were tested in supported schools, with no major incident trend reported in Year 1 monitoring returns. No evidence was reported of funds not used as intended, and hardship grants deduplicated 16 caregiver records before payment. Climate or environmental disruption did not stop delivery in Year 1, although lake-shore transport costs increased for OP1.1. [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:safeguarding_risk_where_relevant;gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:funds_not_used_as_intended_risk;gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:climate_environment_risk]

Overall, performance conclusions for the period were positive but qualified by data timeliness issues and under-delivery on selected indicators linked to attendance follow-up, menstrual health readiness and coordination meetings. The main lesson from the period was that direct service delivery moved faster than some supporting systems for reporting completeness and school-level readiness.

content.text:
Monitoring in Year 1 relied on routine programme records rather than a standalone evaluation. Indicator actuals were drawn from the BridgeLight AR1 export, with source notes recorded per output, and attendance and financial lines included variance explanations. Monitoring used termly indicator returns and partner spot checks. Outcome monitoring also used term attendance registers and school safeguarding pathway checks. No standalone external evaluation was commissioned in Year 1. [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:evidence_base_strength] [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:evaluation_progress] [gap:performance_and_conclusions:table:outcome_assessment]

The submitted evidence base covered several delivery streams. Records cited for verification included school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists, and district validation samples. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures, which supported confidence in the reported result that 684 girls were re-enrolled or retained against a Year 1 target of 650. Evidence for attendance was weaker: 472 girls were reported as attending at least 80% of school days against a target of 500, but four schools submitted attendance registers late, which affected OP1.2 reporting. This means the attendance shortfall should be read with some caution, even though the variance remained visible in submitted records. Evidence quality was mixed across outputs but was generally adequate for annual review purposes. Physical infrastructure and service-delivery outputs were supported by clearer documentary trails than some behaviour-related measures. For example, WASH engineer certificates supported reporting that 31 functional girls' latrine stances were delivered against a Year 1 target of 24. Menstrual health support reached 17 schools against a target of 20, and submitted records explained this variance through menstrual health supply delays. Re-entry support outputs were also well evidenced in the AR1 export and related forms: 571 girls received re-entry kits against a target of 550, while 136 school and community actors were trained on re-entry and safeguarding against a target of 120. [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:new_evidence] [fact:indicators.op2_1_latrine_stances_functional.y1_actual] [fact:indicators.op2_1_latrine_stances_functional.y1_target] [fact:indicators.op2_2_schools_menstrual_health.y1_actual] [fact:indicators.op2_2_schools_menstrual_health.y1_target] [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:new_risks] [fact:indicators.op3_2_girls_reentry_kit.y1_actual] [fact:indicators.op3_2_girls_reentry_kit.y1_target] [fact:indicators.op4_3_actors_trained_reentry.y1_actual] [fact:indicators.op4_3_actors_trained_reentry.y1_target]

There were still important limits to comparability and completeness. Partner returns used a review period of 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25, while the award letter set the first Annual Review period at 2024-10-15 to 2025-10-14; finance had not recut to that window at the point of reporting. That timing mismatch did not invalidate the Year 1 evidence base, but it reduced precision when aligning programme records with FCDO review requirements. The award letter also required disaggregated monitoring data by gender, age and vulnerability, yet exact disaggregation was not available in the submitted records used for this section. In addition, no numeric equity target was stated for reaching girls with disabilities, ultra-poor households or out-of-school girls; only a qualitative expectation was recorded. As a result, this review could comment on evidence sources and reported reach patterns only in limited terms, not test performance against a numeric equity benchmark. Overall, the evidence submitted was sufficient to support a cautious assessment that delivery remained broadly on track across most outputs during Year 1, with stronger confidence in re-enrolment, remedial support, grants administration and infrastructure-related results than in attendance reporting alone. The monitoring system identified both over-performance and shortfalls against targets rather than masking them, which increased credibility. Still, because no external evaluation was commissioned and because some source records arrived late or used a misaligned reporting window, findings should be treated as routine monitoring results with known limitations rather than independently verified impact evidence.

No new material risks were reported beyond those already captured in the grant risk register during the review period. The main delivery issue that materialised was a delay in menstrual health supplies, which affected OP2.2 performance: 17 schools were reached against a Year 1 target of 20. This was a contained variance rather than a wider control failure, and it sat alongside stronger delivery elsewhere, including 31 functional girls’ latrine stances against a target of 24 and 136 school and community actors trained on re-entry and safeguarding against a target of 120. That points to functioning pre-payment checks rather than post hoc correction alone. [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:funds_not_used_as_intended_risk]

Environmental and operating conditions created some cost pressure but did not stop delivery. Lake-shore transport costs increased for OP1.1, and Year 1 spend on that line reached GBP 174,850 against a budget of GBP 162,000. Even so, no major climate shock stopped delivery in Year 1, and OP1.1 still exceeded target performance with 684 girls re-enrolled or retained against a target of 650. This suggests that the programme absorbed local cost pressure while maintaining service delivery, though at higher unit cost on that line than planned. [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:climate_environment_risk] [fact:financials.lines.op1_1.y1_actual] [fact:financials.lines.op1_1.y1_budget] [fact:indicators.op1_1_girls_reenrolled_retained.y1_actual] [fact:indicators.op1_1_girls_reenrolled_retained.y1_target]

Safeguarding controls remained active through the period. Referral pathways were tested in supported schools, and Year 1 monitoring returns did not report any major incident trend. Training also supported these controls: 136 school and community actors were trained on re-entry and safeguarding against a target of 120. While this does not remove safeguarding risk, it indicates that referral arrangements were exercised and frontline actors received more coverage than planned under the Year 1 target. [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:safeguarding_risk_where_relevant] [fact:indicators.op4_3_actors_trained_reentry.y1_actual] [fact:indicators.op4_3_actors_trained_reentry.y1_target]

A cross-cutting control issue remained around reporting quality rather than misuse or safeguarding failure. Partner returns used a review window of 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25, while the award letter set the first Annual Review period at 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025, and finance had not yet recut to that window. In addition, four schools submitted attendance registers late, which affected OP1.2 reporting; attendance at 80% or above was reported at 472 against a target of 500. These issues limited precision in reporting but did not amount to evidence of fraud or major safeguarding breakdown. They do show where management attention was still needed to align records fully with FCDO requirements for disaggregated monitoring data and Annual Review reporting timelines. content.text:
Value for money in Year 1 was assessed against economy, efficiency, effectiveness and equity using the Annual Review evidence base. The programme spent GBP 920,420 against a Year 1 budget of GBP 880,000, so total spend was above plan for the period. This variance sat alongside mixed movement across output lines rather than uniform overspend. [fact:financials.y1_actual.total][fact:financials.y1_budget.total]

On economy, several lines ran close to plan, while others exceeded budget. OP1.3 spent GBP 81,330 against GBP 88,000, OP2.2 spent GBP 39,600 against GBP 42,000, OP3.3 spent GBP 24,980 against GBP 31,000 and OP4.1 spent GBP 32,700 against GBP 39,000. These underspends partly offset higher costs on OP1.1 at GBP 174,850 against GBP 162,000, OP1.2 at GBP 98,740 against GBP 94,000, OP2.1 at GBP 148,900 against GBP 121,000, OP3.1 at GBP 151,440 against GBP 146,000, OP3.2 at GBP 109,250 against GBP 103,000 and OP4.3 at GBP 58,630 against GBP 54,000. A stated cost driver was increased lake-shore transport costs for OP1.1; no major climate shock stopped delivery in Year 1. There was also no evidence that funds were used other than intended, and hardship grant payment checks removed duplicate risk in 16 caregiver records before payment. [fact:financials.lines.op1_3.y1_actual][fact:financials.lines.op1_3.y1_budget][fact:financials.lines.op2_2.y1_actual][fact:financials.lines.op2_2.y1_budget][fact:financials.lines.op3_3.y1_actual][fact:financials.lines.op3_3.y1_budget][fact:financials.lines.op4_1.y1_actual][fact:financials.lines.op4_1.y1_budget][fact:financials.lines.op1_1.y1_actual][fact:financials.lines.op1_1.y1_budget][fact:financials.lines.op1_2.y1_actual][fact:financials.lines.op1_2.y1_budget][fact:financials.lines.op2_1.y1_actual][fact:financials.lines.op2_1.y1_budget][fact:financials.lines.op3_1.y1_actual][fact:financials.lines.op3_1.y1_budget][fact:financials.lines.op3_2.y1_actual][fact:financials.lines.op3_2.y1_budget][fact:financials.lines.op4_3.y1_actual][fact:financials.lines.op4_3.y1_budget][gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:climate_environment_risk][gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:funds_not_used_as_intended_risk]

On efficiency, delivery converted spending into results well on a number of outputs. Re-enrolment or retention reached 684 girls against a target of 650; remedial sessions reached 438 girls against a target of 420; functional girls' latrine stances reached 31 against a target of 24; re-entry kits reached 571 girls against a target of 550; and training on re-entry and safeguarding reached 136 actors against a target of 120. At the same time, attendance at or above eighty per cent reached 472 girls against a target of 500; caregivers receiving hardship grants reached 392 against a target of 400; district learning meetings reached three against a target of four; schools with menstrual health supplies and trained teachers reached seventeen against a target of twenty; and follow-up among hardship households stood at 0.68 in Year 1 compared with an endline target of eighty-five per cent recorded in the proposal export set. The available explanation for weaker performance on attendance was late register submission from four schools. For OP2.2, menstrual health supply delays affected delivery and three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training. [fact:indicators.op1_11_girls_reenrolled_retained.y11_target]

sections.label: F. Programme Management: Delivery, Commercial and Financial Performance

content.text:
Delivery remained broadly on track during the review period, with district validation samples confirming re-entry figures, although late register submission from four schools affected attendance reporting [gap:programme_management_delivery_commercial_financial:indicator:partner_performance]. Results data reflected this mixed picture. OP1.1 reached 684 girls re-enrolled or retained against a Year 1 target of 650, while OP1.2 reached 472 girls attending at least 80% of school days against a target of 500 [fact:indicators.op1_1_girls_reenrolled_retained.y1_actual, fact:indicators.op1_1_girls_reenrolled_retained.y1_target, fact:indicators.op1_2_girls_attending_80pct.y1_actual, fact:indicators.op1_2_girls_attending_80pct.y1_target]. Infrastructure and support outputs were also largely delivered: OP2.1 reported 31 functional girls latrine stances against a target of 24, OP3.2 reached 571 girls receiving re-entry kits against a target of 550, and OP4.3 trained 136 school and community actors on re-entry and safeguarding against a target of 120 [fact:indicators.op2_1_latrine_stances_functional.y1_actual, fact:indicators.op2_1_latrine_stances_functional.y1_target, fact:indicators.op3_2_girls_reentry_kit.y1_actual, fact:indicators.op3_2_girls_reentry_kit.y1_target, fact:indicators.op4_3_actors_trained_reentry.y1_actual, fact:indicators.op4_3_actors_trained_reentry.y1_target]. The main delivery gap sat in OP2.2, where menstrual health supplies and trained teachers were in place in 17 schools against a target of 20; records attribute this shortfall to menstrual health supply delays [fact:indicators.op2_2_schools_menstrual_health.y1_actual, fact:indicators.op2_2_schools_menstrual_health.y1_target, gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:new_risks].

Financial performance was above the Year 1 budget allocation recorded in the AR1 export. Total Year 1 actual spend was GBP 920,420 against a Year 1 budget of GBP 880,000 [fact:financials.y1_actual.total, fact:financials.y1_budget.total]. At line level, overspends were recorded on OP1.1 at GBP 174,850 against GBP 162,000, OP2.1 at GBP 148,900 against GBP 121,000, OP3.1 at GBP 151,440 against GBP 146,000, OP3.2 at GBP 109,250 against GBP 103,000, and OP4.3 at GBP 58,630 against GBP 54,000 [fact:financials.lines.op1_1.y1_actual, fact:financials.lines.op1_1.y1_budget, fact:financials.lines.op2_1.y1_actual, fact:financials.lines.op2_1.y1_budget, fact:financials.lines.op3_1.y1_actual, fact:financials.lines.op3_2.y1_budget? wait]
assumptions: No evidence was available for supplier or consultant performance; the section therefore did not assess that indicator beyond noting the gap.
No specific commercial or procurement issue was provided in the submitted facts beyond menstrual health supply delays affecting OP2.2.

A sampled-line financial summary appears in gap answer programme_management_delivery_commercial_financial:indicator:financial_delivery but does not reconcile with the full Year 0 total budget and actual figures from the ARI export; narrative therefore used the full financial facts for spend versus budget.

The submitted records show a reporting-period mismatch between partner returns and the award letter review window; this was described as a data quality and management issue rather than recasting figures.

content.text:
Recommendations in this review were tied to the main delivery and reporting issues recorded during Year 1. Previous review actions on register cleaning were partially complete, and September deduplication removed double-count risk on OP1.1. However, late attendance data still affected reporting quality, with four schools submitting registers late. The review therefore prioritised three corrective actions: recutting finance to the FCDO review window of 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025, completing menstrual health training in the three remaining schools, and securing submission of the late attendance registers. These priorities aligned with the wider next-period focus to close the OP2.2 gap at 17 of 20 schools, complete disposal bins at four latrine units, and correct reporting-period labelling against the award letter. [gap:recommendations_and_actions:indicator:updates_on_previous_recommendations] [gap:recommendations_and_actions:indicator:recommendations_from_current_review] [gap:recommendations_and_actions:indicator:priorities_for_next_period] [fact:reporting.annual_review_period_1.start] [fact:reporting.annual_review_period_1.end]

The action plan below reflected named owners in the submitted records. The Programme Manager was assigned to recut the AR1 period by Q1 next period. M&E was assigned to follow up with the four schools for Term 3 registers. WASH was assigned to finish disposal bins. Exact due dates beyond Q1 next period were not available in the submitted records, so they were left unspecified rather than inferred. content.text:
This Annual Review covered the period 2025-04-01 to 2026-03-31. Year 1 delivery remained broadly on track against the results framework, with stronger performance on re-enrolment and school WASH infrastructure than planned, and some slippage on attendance follow-up and menstrual health support in a minority of schools [gap:summary_and_overview:indicator:overall_progress][fact:indicators.OP1.1.ar1_actual][fact:indicators.OP1.1.ar1_milestone_target][fact:indicators.OP2.1.ar1_actual][fact:indicators.OP2.1.ar1_milestone_target][fact:indicators.OP3.3.ar1_actual][fact:indicators.OP3.3.ar1_milestone_target][fact:indicators.OP2.2.ar1_actual][fact:indicators.OP2.2.ar1_milestone_target].

Against Output 1, the programme reported 684 girls re-enrolled against a Year 1 milestone of 650, 472 girls attending at least 80% of school days against a milestone of 500, and 438 girls completing at least 20 remedial sessions against a milestone of 420 [fact:indicators.OP1.1.ar1_actual][fact:indicators.OP1.1.ar1_milestone_target][fact:indicators.OP1.2.ar1_actual][fact:indicators.OP1.2.ar1_milestone_target][fact:indicators.OP1.3.ar1_actual][fact:indicators.OP1.3.ar1_milestone_target]. Against Output 2, delivery exceeded the Year 1 milestone for latrine stances, with 31 completed against 24, while menstrual health support reached 17 schools against a milestone of 20 [fact:indicators.OP2.1.ar1_actual][fact:indicators.OP2.1.ar1_milestone_target][fact:indicators.OP2.2.ar1_actual][fact:indicators.OP2.2.ar1_milestone_target]. Against Output 3, the programme reached 392 caregivers with hardship grants against a milestone of 400, provided 571 girls with school re-entry kits against a milestone of 550, and recorded verified attendance follow-up for 0.68 of hardship grant households against a milestone of 0.75 [fact:indicators.OP3.1.ar1_actual][fact:indicators.OP3.1.ar1_milestone_target][fact:indicators.OP3.2.ar1_actual][fact:indicators.OP3.2.ar1_milestone_target][fact:indicators.OP3.3.ar1_actual][fact:indicators.OP3.3.ar1_milestone_target]. Against Output 4, the programme held 3 district learning meetings against a milestone of 4 and trained 136 school and community actors against a milestone of 120 [fact:indicators.OP4.1.ar1_actual][fact:indicators.OP4.0?]
