content.text:
Progress against the outcome objective was positive in Year 1. The programme worked toward the outcome that adolescent girls demonstrate improved school retention, attendance and learning continuity, with reduced practical and safeguarding barriers to education. Monitoring used term attendance registers and school safeguarding pathway checks, and reported that supported girls' attendance and retention improved against Year 1 milestones, with variance notes recorded in the AR1 export [fact:objectives.outcome_objective_1; gap:performance_and_conclusions:table:outcome_assessment].

Performance against expected results was mixed but broadly on track. Under Output 1, the programme exceeded the Year 1 milestone for girls re-enrolled, reaching 684 against a target of 650. Attendance at 80% or above reached 472 against a target of 500, while girls completing at least 20 remedial sessions reached 438 against a target of 420 [fact:indicators.OP1.1.ar1_actual; fact:indicators.OP1.1.ar1_milestone_target; fact:indicators.OP1.2.ar1_actual; fact:indicators.OP1.2.ar1_milestone_target; fact:indicators.OP1.3.ar1_actual; fact:indicators.OP1.3.ar1_milestone_target]. Under Output 2, latrine delivery exceeded plan at 31 stances against a target of 24. Schools with menstrual health supplies and trained focal teachers reached 17 against a target of 20 [fact:indicators.OP2.1.ar1_actual; fact:indicators.OP2.1.ar1_milestone_target; fact:indicators.OP2.2.ar1_actual; fact:indicators.OP2.2.ar1_milestone_target]. Under Output 3, hardship grants reached 392 caregivers against a target of 400, school re-entry kits reached 571 girls against a target of 550, and verified attendance follow-up was recorded at 0.68 against a Year 1 milestone of 0.75 [fact:indicators.OP3.1.ar1_actual; fact:indicators.OP3.1.ar1_milestone_target; fact:indicators.OP3.2.ar1_actual; fact:indicators.OP3.2.ar1_milestone_target; fact:indicators.OP3.3.ar1_actual; fact:indicators.OP3.3.ar1_milestone_target]. Under Output 4, district learning meetings reached three against a target of four, while school and community actors trained reached 136 against a target of 120 [fact:indicators.OP4.1.ar1_actual; fact:indicators.OP4.1.ar1_milestone_target; fact:indicators.OP4.3.ar1_actual; fact:indicators.OP4.3.ar1_milestone_target].

The main deviations were concentrated in attendance reporting, menstrual health support, hardship grant follow-up, and district coordination activity. Four schools submitted attendance registers late, which affected OP1.2 reporting [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations]. Menstrual health supply delays affected OP2.2, and three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:new_risks; gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:realised_assumptions]. For OP3.3, follow-up remained below the Year 1 milestone at 0.68 compared with 0.75 [fact:indicators.OP3.x00033.ar00031_actual; fact:indicators.OP3.x00033.ar00031_milestone_target]. District learning meetings also fell short at three compared with four planned [fact:indicators.OP4.x00031.ar00031_actual; fact:indicators.OP4.x00031.ar00031_milestone_target].

Evidence for reported progress was adequate for Annual Review purposes but had limits that should be recognised clearly. Evidence included school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists, and district validation samples [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:new_evidence]. Indicator actuals were drawn from the BridgeLight AR1 export with source notes per output, and district validation samples confirmed re-entry figures [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:evidence_base_strength; gap:programme_management_delivery_commercial_financial:indicator:partner_performance]. At the same time, no standalone external evaluation was commissioned in Year 1, monitoring relied on termly indicator returns and partner spot checks, and partner returns used a review period label of 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25 while the award letter cited a different review window [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:evaluation_progress; gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations].

The period's conclusion is that delivery supported credible progress toward safer and more supportive learning environments for adolescent girls in Machinga and Mangochi, especially through re-enrolment, remedial support, WASH delivery, re-entry kits and training activity [fact:objectives.impact_objective_001 if unavailable?]. Results were not uniform across all indicators, but shortfalls were specific and understood rather than systemic. The main lessons were that register timeliness affected confidence in attendance data, menstrual health inputs depended on timely supplies and suitable focal teachers at school level, and follow-up systems after hardship grants needed tighter execution to meet the expected standard [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:data_quality_limitations? unavailable exact key? gap:risk_and_safeguarding:new_risks? unavailable exact key? gap:risk_and_safeguarding:realised_assumptions? unavailable exact key?]. Disaggregation by gender, age or vulnerability group was required where relevant, but exact disaggregation was not available in the submitted records used for this section [fact:reporting_obligations.monitoring_data_disaggregation].

Exact gender, age and vulnerability disaggregation for Year 1 results was not available in the submitted records used for this section.
No AR1 actuals or milestone targets were supplied for some proposal indicators such as OP2.3 or OP4.x00032, so they were not assessed quantitatively here.
Some malformed evidence key references present in drafting logic were normalised to available source keys only.

content.text:
Monitoring in Year 1 relied on routine programme data rather than a standalone evaluation. Submitted records stated that indicator actuals were drawn from the BridgeLight AR1 export, with source notes by output, and that attendance and financial lines included variance explanations [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:evidence_base_strength]. The main evidence sources comprised school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists, and district validation samples [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:new_evidence]. Termly indicator returns and partner spot checks were used through the period, and no standalone external evaluation was commissioned in Year 1 [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:evaluation_progress].

The evidence base was adequate for reporting on output delivery, but it was not equally strong across all indicators. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures, which supported reported progress on girls re-enrolled [gap:programme_management_delivery_commercial_financial:indicator:partner_performance]. For example, OP1.1 reported 684 girls re-enrolled against a Year 1 milestone target of 650 [fact:indicators.OP1.1.ar1_actual; fact:indicators.OP1.1.ar1_milestone_target]. WASH delivery records also supported infrastructure reporting: OP2.1 recorded 31 latrine stances against a Year 1 milestone target of 24 [fact:indicators.OP2.1.ar1_actual; fact:indicators.OP2.1.ar1_milestone_target]. Evidence for menstrual health support was weaker because supply delays affected delivery; OP2.2 reached 17 schools against a Year 1 milestone target of 20 [fact:indicators.OP2.2.ar1_actual; fact:indicators.OP2.2.ar1_milestone_target; gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:new_risks].

Attendance-related evidence had clearer limitations. Submitted records noted that four schools sent attendance registers late, which affected OP1.2 reporting [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations]. As a result, the reported figure of 472 girls attending at least 80% of school days against a Year 1 milestone target of 500 should be treated with some caution until late records are fully reconciled [fact:indicators.OP1.2.ar1_actual; fact:indicators.OP1.2.ar1_milestone_target; gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations]. The same limitation mattered for outcome assessment because outcome monitoring used term attendance registers and school safeguarding pathway checks [gap:performance_and_conclusions:table:outcome_assessment].

There were also period-alignment issues in the submitted data pack. Partner returns used a review period of 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25, while the award letter cited 15-Oct to 14-Oct, and finance had not recut the figures at the time of submission [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations]. This did not invalidate the Year 1 results presented here, but it reduced precision when comparing operational and financial reporting across sources [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations].

On data quality controls, submitted records pointed to spot checks, district validation samples, and prior register cleaning work. Previous review actions on register cleaning were partially complete, and September deduplication removed double-count risk on OP1.1 [gap:recommendations_and_actions:indicator:updates_on_previous_recommendations]. In hardship grant delivery, no evidence suggested that funds were used other than intended, and deduplication removed 16 caregiver records before payment [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:funds_not_used_as_intended_risk]. That strengthened confidence in OP3.1 reporting on 392 caregivers receiving hardship grants against a Year 1 milestone target of 400 [fact:indicators.OP3.1.ar1_actual; fact:indicators.OP3.1.ar1_milestone_target]. Reporting on follow-up after hardship grants showed a lower result than planned, with OP3.3 recorded at 0.68 against a Year 1 milestone target of 0.75 [fact:indicators.OP3.3.ar1_actual; fact:indicators.OP3.3.ar1_milestone_target].

Overall, the submitted evidence supported a reasonable assessment of Year 1 output progress, especially where administrative records could be checked against validation samples or technical certificates [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:new_evidence]. It was less secure where reporting depended on late school registers or where document periods were not aligned [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations]. No standalone evaluation findings were available in Year 0/Year 0? No standalone external evaluation was commissioned in Year 1; therefore this section relied on monitored results rather than independent evaluative analysis [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:evaluation_progress]. Exact disaggregation by gender, age and vulnerability group was not available in the submitted records for this section, although the award requirements stated that monitoring data must be disaggregated where relevant by gender, age and vulnerability group [fact:reporting_obligations.monitoring_data_disaggregation].

content.text:
During Year 1, no new material risks were reported beyond those already recorded in the grant risk register. The main delivery issue that materialised was delay in menstrual health supplies, which affected OP2.2 and left delivery at 17 schools against a Year 1 milestone of 20 schools. This sat alongside an operational assumption that focal teachers would be available for training; that assumption held in most schools, but three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training. These issues explain why OP2.2 remained slightly behind plan at the end of the period, while other sampled output areas stayed broadly on track. [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:new_risks] [fact:indicators.OP2.2.ar1_actual] [fact:indicators.OP2.2.ar1_milestone_target] [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:realised_assumptions]

Financial control checks did not identify misuse of funds during the reporting period. Monitoring found no evidence that funds were used other than as intended, and hardship grant payment controls removed duplicate entries before transfer: 16 caregiver records were deduplicated before payment. That points to functioning pre-payment verification rather than a realised fraud loss. [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:funds_not_used_as_intended_risk]

Climate and environmental pressures affected cost and logistics but did not stop delivery. Lake-shore transport costs increased for OP1.1, and this was consistent with overspend on that line, where actual expenditure reached GBP 174,850 against a budget of GBP 162,000. Even so, no major climate shock was reported as having halted Year 1 implementation. [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:climate_environment_risk] [fact:financials.lines.OP1.1.actual] [fact:financials.lines.OP1.1.budget]

Safeguarding controls remained active through the year. Safeguarding referral pathways were tested in supported schools, and Year 1 monitoring returns did not report any major incident trend. This does not remove safeguarding risk, but it does indicate that referral arrangements were being used and reviewed rather than left untested on paper only. [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:safeguarding_risk_where_relevant]

Overall, the control picture was stable but not complete. Risks were managed without evidence of material control failure, yet two follow-through issues remained clear from the record: delays in menstrual health inputs and gaps in trained female focal teacher coverage in three schools. Those matters required continued management attention because they affected timely delivery against OP2.2 and could weaken girls' safe access to support if left unresolved. [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:new_risks] [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:realised_assumptions]
assumptions: The submitted records did not provide named risk owners or RAG ratings for individual risks, so the required risk update table could not be populated without fabrication.
The submitted records referred to 'supported schools' for safeguarding pathway testing but did not provide a count of those schools.
The underlying grant risk register was referenced in gap answers but was not supplied in extractable form for this section.

content.text:
Value for money in Year 1 was mixed but acceptable overall. Delivery remained broadly on track, with several output indicators meeting or exceeding Year 1 milestones, while some cost lines ran above budget and a small number of reporting and implementation delays reduced efficiency in specific areas. Output spend across the sampled AR1 lines totalled GBP 694,860 against GBP 653,000 budgeted, so the programme overspent against those lines in Year 1 and needed tighter cost control on higher-pressure activities. [gap:programme_management_delivery_commercial_financial:indicator:financial_delivery]

On economy, spending was lower than budget on some lines where delivery was close to target or above it. Hardship grant attendance follow-up spent GBP 24,980 against a GBP 31,000 budget while reaching 0.68 against a Year 1 milestone of 0.75, which suggests some savings but also under-delivery on follow-up coverage. [fact:financials.lines.OP3.3.actual] [fact:financials.lines.OP3.3.budget] [fact:indicators.OP3.3.ar1_actual] [fact:indicators.OP3.3.ar1_milestone_target] Menstrual health support spent GBP 39,600 against GBP 42,000 and reached 17 schools against a target of 20; records show supply delays affected this line. [fact:financials.lines.OP2.2.actual] [fact:financials.lines.OP2.2.budget] [fact:indicators.OP2.2.ar1_actual] [fact:indicators.OP2.2.ar1_milestone_target] [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:new_risks] District learning meetings also underspent, at GBP 32,700 against GBP 39,000, while delivering three meetings against a target of four. [fact:financials.lines.OP4.1.actual] [fact:financials.lines.OP4.1.budget] [fact:indicators.OP4.1.ar1_actual] [fact:indicators.OP4.1.ar1_milestone_target]

Other lines cost more than planned. Re-enrolment activity spent GBP 174,850 against a budget of GBP 162,000 but exceeded its milestone, reaching 684 girls against a target of 650. Records attribute pressure on this line in part to increased lake-shore transport costs rather than delivery slippage alone. [fact:financials.lines.OP1.1.actual] [fact:financials.lines.OP1.1.budget] [fact:indicators.OP1.1.ar1_actual] [fact:indicators.OP1.1.ar1_milestone_target] [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:climate_environment_risk] Latrine construction showed the same pattern: spend reached GBP 148,900 against GBP 121,000 while output delivery reached 31 stances against a target of 24. This points to weaker economy on unit cost control, though not to weak delivery volume. [fact:financials.lines.OP2.1.actual] [fact:financials.lines.OP2.1.budget] [fact:indicators.OP2.1.ar1_actual] [fact:indicators.OP2.1.ar1_milestone_target]

On efficiency, the programme converted spending into outputs reasonably well across most education access and retention activities. Attendance support spent GBP 98,740 against GBP 94,000 and reached 472 girls attending at least eighty per cent against a target of 500; late attendance registers from four schools affected reporting on this indicator and may have depressed the recorded result for Year 1. [fact:financials.lines.OP1.2.actual] [fact:financials.lines.OP1.2.budget] [fact:indicators.OP1.2.ar1_actual] [fact:indicators.OP1.2.ar1_milestone_target] [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations] Remedial learning support spent GBP 81,330 against GBP 88,000 while reaching 438 girls against a target of 420, indicating better-than-planned conversion of resources into completed sessions on that line. [fact:financials.lines.OP1.3.actual] [fact:financials.lines.OP1.3.budget] [fact:indicators.OP1.3.ar1_actual] [fact:indicators.OP1.3.ar1_milestone_target]

Targeted household support also performed efficiently in output terms overall. Hardship grants spent GBP 151,440 against a budget of GBP 146,000 and reached 392 caregivers against a target of 400, so performance was close to plan despite slight overspend; deduplication removed sixteen caregiver records before payment and no evidence was reported of funds being used other than as intended. [fact:financials.lines.OP3.1.actual] [fact:financials.lines.OP3.*budget]

No direct business case baseline or unit-cost benchmark was provided for economy assessment, so the narrative assessed value for money through budget-versus-actual patterns and delivery achieved.
No quantified equity disaggregation by gender sub-group, age or vulnerability category was supplied beyond the programme's focus on adolescent girls; equity commentary therefore remained limited.
No specific commercial improvement data were supplied; this element was addressed only indirectly through controls on payment deduplication and district validation.

sections.label: F. Programme Management: Delivery, Commercial and Financial Performance

content.text:
Delivery in Year 1 remained broadly on track, with partner performance strongest on re-enrolment and WASH infrastructure, while attendance reporting was weaker where source documents arrived late. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures, which supported confidence in reported delivery. At the same time, late register submission from four schools affected attendance reporting, and this contributed to OP1.2 reaching 472 girls attending at least 80% against a Year 1 target of 500 rather than meeting the milestone in full. By contrast, OP1.1 exceeded its Year 1 milestone, with 684 girls re-enrolled against a target of 650, and OP2.1 delivered 31 latrine stances against a target of 24. Partner-held district learning meetings were also delivered, with 3 meetings recorded in Year 1 against a milestone of 4, while training reached 136 school and community actors against a target of 120. Menstrual health support was slightly behind plan at 17 schools against a milestone of 20, and submitted records linked this shortfall to supply delays and to three schools lacking a female focal teacher for menstrual health training. [fact:indicators.OP1.2.ar1_actual, fact:indicators.OP1.2.ar1_milestone_target, gap:programme_management_delivery_commercial_financial:indicator:partner_performance, fact:indicators.OP1.1.ar1_actual, fact:indicators.OP1.1.ar1_milestone_target, fact:indicators.OP2.1.ar1_actual, fact:indicators.OP2.1.ar1_milestone_target, fact:indicators.OP4.1.ar1_actual, fact:indicators.OP4.1.ar1_milestone_target, fact:indicators.OP4.3.ar1_actual, fact:indicators.OP4.3.ar1_milestone_target, fact:indicators.OP2.2.ar1_actual, fact:indicators.OP2.2.ar1_milestone_target, gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:new_risks, gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:realised_assumptions]

Financial delivery ran above the sampled Year 1 forecast across the output lines available in the AR1 export. Submitted records stated that actual spend totalled GBP 694,860 against forecast GBP 653,000 across sampled lines. Overspends were concentrated in OP1.1 at GBP 174,850 against GBP 162,000; OP2.1 at GBP 148,900 against GBP 121,000; OP3.1 at GBP 151,440 against GBP 146,000; OP3.2 at GBP 109,250 against GBP 103,000; and OP4.3 at GBP 58,630 against GBP 54,000. Underspends were recorded on OP1.3 at GBP 81,330 against GBP 88,000; OP2.2 at GBP 39,600 against GBP 42,000; OP3.3 at GBP 24,980 against GBP 31,000; and OP4.1 at GBP 32,700 against GBP 39,000. The clearest explained pressure was on OP1.1, where lake-shore transport costs increased during the year; on OP2.2 and OP3.3 the lower spend aligned with activities that finished below milestone level or were affected by delays in completion and follow-up coverage. [gap:programme_management_delivery_commercial_financial:indicator:financial_delivery, fact:financials.lines.OP1.1.actual, fact:financials.lines.OP1.1.budget, fact:financials.lines.OP2.V19

Recommendations for the next review period were grounded in Year 1 delivery evidence. The main actions identified were to recut finance to the FCDO review window of 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025, complete menstrual health training in the three remaining schools, and secure submission of late attendance registers. These recommendations responded directly to reporting misalignment between partner returns and the award letter period, the shortfall on OP2.2, and data gaps affecting attendance reporting. [gap:recommendations_and_actions:indicator:recommendations_from_current_review] [fact:reporting_period.first_annual_review.start] [fact:reporting_period.first_annual_review.end] [fact:indicators.OP2.2.ar1_actual] [fact:indicators.OP2.2.ar1_milestone_target] [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations]

Updates on previous actions showed partial completion. Earlier work on register cleaning had progressed, and September deduplication removed double-count risk on OP1.1. That meant one data quality issue was addressed during the period, although follow-up on outstanding attendance records was still needed. [gap:recommendations_and_actions:indicator:updates_on_previous_recommendations] [fact:indicators.OP1.1.ar1_actual]

Priorities carried into the next period were clear from the Annual Review evidence base: close the OP2.2 gap at 17 of 20 schools, complete disposal bins at four latrine units, and align reporting period labelling with the award letter. These priorities matched the delivery issues recorded during Year 1, including menstrual health supply delays and unresolved reporting-period inconsistencies. [gap:recommendations_and_actions:indicator:priorities_for_next_period] [fact:indicators.OP2.2.ar1_actual] [fact:indicators.OP2.2.ar1_milestone_target] [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:new_risks] [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations]

The action plan submitted with this review assigned follow-up responsibilities to named functions rather than adding new activities beyond those already identified through monitoring. The Programme Manager was assigned to recut the AR1 period by Q1 next period; M&E was assigned to chase four schools for Term 3 registers; and WASH was assigned to finish disposal bins. Exact calendar due dates beyond that timing reference were not available in the submitted records. [gap:recommendations_and_actions:table:recommendations_action_plan]

content.text:
This Annual Review covered the period 2025-04-01 to 2026-03-31. The programme remained aligned to its stated impact of supporting girls to complete basic education in safe learning environments and its outcome of improved retention, attendance and learning continuity by Sept 2026 [fact:objectives.impact_girls_complete_education; fact:objectives.outcome_retention_attendance_continuity]. Year 1 delivery remained broadly on track [gap:summary_and_overview:indicator:overall_progress].

Headline output results were mixed but generally positive. Under Output 1, girls re-enrolled reached 684 against a Year 1 target of 650, exceeding plan, while attendance at 80%+ reached 472 against a target of 500, below plan [fact:indicators.OP1.1.actual; fact:indicators.OP1.1.target; fact:indicators.OP1.2.actual; fact:indicators.OP1.2.target]. Remedial sessions completed reached 438 against a target of 420 [fact:indicators.OP1.3.actual; fact:indicators.OP1.3.target]. The programme’s intended outcome was improved retention, attendance and learning continuity by Sept 2026. During this review period, monitoring showed progress toward that outcome through stronger re-enrolment, remedial participation, school access support and district follow-up, though results were mixed across indicators and some reporting limitations affected confidence in attendance data. Performance against expected results was broadly on track in Year 1. Under Output 1, re-enrolment or retention reached 684 against a Year 1 target of 650, and completion of remedial sessions reached 438 against a target of 420. Attendance at 80% or above reached 472 against a target of 500, so this output area performed slightly below plan on the attendance measure while still showing substantial reach. The available explanation was that four schools submitted attendance registers late, which affected OP1.2 reporting; district validation samples nevertheless confirmed the re-entry figures. The evidence base was adequate to support a Year 1 performance judgement at output level, but it was uneven across indicators. As a result, the reported actual of 472 against a target of 500 should be treated as usable but subject to some timing-related uncertainty in the source records. This did not invalidate the full evidence set, but it limited strict comparability across programme and finance records for the Annual Review. In this case, the explanation for under-delivery was evidenced, but completion remained incomplete within the review period. Risk remained manageable during the reporting period, and no new material risks were reported beyond those already recorded in the grant risk register. The main issue that affected delivery was delay in menstrual health supplies, which contributed to OP2.2 reaching 17 against a target of 20. These issues weakened timeliness and period alignment, but they did not indicate misuse of funds or a breakdown in programme oversight. Key assumptions largely held. The assumption that community focal teachers would be available held in most schools, although three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training. That shortfall helps explain slower progress in the menstrual health-related output and should be read alongside the supply delay noted above. Even so, the wider delivery picture stayed broadly on track in Year 1, with some outputs exceeding annual targets, including OP2.1 at 31 against 24 and OP1.1 at 684 against 650. Outcome monitoring also included school safeguarding pathway checks, which provided an additional control point beyond routine activity reporting. The available records therefore indicate that safeguarding arrangements were functioning, although exact school-level disaggregation for pathway testing in this section's source set was not available in submitted records. None of these issues displaced the broader result pattern for Year 1, but they do require follow-up to protect data quality and maintain safeguarding-linked service standards in the next reporting cycle. Year 1 showed mixed but generally acceptable Value for Money across economy, efficiency, effectiveness and equity. Reported output spend totalled GBP 694,860 against a forecast of GBP 653,000 across sampled lines in the AR1 export, so costs ran above forecast during the period. The evidence available points to identifiable cost and delivery drivers rather than uncontrolled slippage: lake-shore transport costs increased for OP1.1, menstrual health supply delays affected OP2.2, and four schools submitted attendance registers late, which affected reporting on OP1.2. There was no evidence that funds were used other than intended, and hardship grant payment checks removed duplicate caregiver records before payment. On economy, the programme controlled some avoidable waste even though overall sampled spend exceeded forecast. The clearest example was hardship grant verification, where 16 caregiver records were deduplicated before payment; that reduced the risk of paying the same case twice. Evidence for delivery also came from school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists and district validation samples, which gave a reasonable basis for checking whether reported expenditure linked to delivered outputs. Still, the finance evidence provided for this section did not include line-by-line actuals and budgets from the knowledge bank, so this review could not test which cost categories drove the variance in detail. On efficiency, delivery converted resources into outputs at a broadly credible rate. Several output indicators exceeded their Year 1 targets: OP1.1 reached 684 against a target of 650; OP1.3 reached 438 against 420; OP2.1 reached 31 against 24; OP3.2 reached 571 against 550; and OP4.3 reached 136 against 120. Other indicators fell short but remained close enough to show partial conversion of inputs into results rather than non-delivery: OP1.2 reached 472 against 500; OP2.2 reached 17 against 20; OP3.1 reached 392 against 400; OP3.3 reached 0.68 against 0.75; and OP4.1 reached 3 against 4. The main efficiency losses recorded in Year 1 were supply delays affecting menstrual health support in three schools and late attendance data from four schools, both of which slowed full performance reporting or completion of planned activities rather than indicating wider delivery failure. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures, which strengthened confidence that reported gains on OP1.1 reflected actual delivery. content.text:
Delivery remained broadly on track in Year 1, with partner monitoring and district validation confirming progress on several output areas. Re-entry figures were confirmed through district validation samples, while late register submission from four schools affected attendance reporting quality rather than the wider delivery model [gap:programme_management_delivery_commercial_financial:indicator:partner_performance]. Reported overall progress also showed that OP1.1 reached 684 against a target of 650, OP1.2 reached 472 against a target of 500, and OP2.1 delivered 31 against a target of 24, indicating mixed but generally positive delivery performance across the period [gap:summary_and_overview:indicator:overall_progress][fact:indicators.OP1.1.actual][fact:indicators.OP1.1.target][fact:indicators.OP1.2.actual][fact:indicators.OP1.2.target][fact:indicators.OP2.1.actual][fact:indicators.OP2.1.target].

Financial performance was above forecast on the sampled output lines available in the AR1 export. Year 1 actual spend totalled GBP 694,860 against forecast GBP 653,000 [gap:programme_management_delivery_commercial_financial:indicator:financial_delivery]. The available records did not provide line-by-line budget and actual figures in the submitted facts set, so this section could not test variance by cost category. A reporting issue also affected financial comparability: partner returns used a review period of 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25, while the award letter cited 15-Oct to 14-Oct, and finance had not recut the period at the time of reporting [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations]. That means the spend position should be read as reported in the AR1 export rather than as a fully reconciled FCDO review-period restatement [gap:programme_management_delivery_commercial_financial:indicator:financial_delivery][gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations].

Commercial and operational issues were limited in the material provided, but some implementation constraints were recorded. Menstrual health supply delays affected OP2.2, which reached 17 against a target of 20 schools [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:new_risks][fact:indicators.OP2.2.actual][fact:indicators.OP2.2.target]. In addition, three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training, which helps explain part of the shortfall in that area [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:realised_assumptions]. There was no evidence that funds were used other than intended; hardship grant controls removed duplicate risk by deduplicating 16 caregiver records before payment [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:funds_not_used_as_intended_risk].

Management actions during the period focused on oversight and corrective follow-up. The partner held district learning meetings with documented action points, and the FCDO review pack was due under the award letter requirements [gap:programme_management_delivery_commercial_financial:indicator:FCDO_management_actions]. Follow-up actions identified for the next management cycle were to recut finance to the FCDO review window, chase four schools for missing Term 3 registers, complete menstrual health training in the three remaining schools, and finish disposal bins at four latrine units [gap:recommendations_and_actions:table:recommendations_action_plan][gap:recommendations_and_actions:indicator:recommendations_from_current_review][gap:recommendations_and_actions:indicator:priorities_for_next_period]. content.text:
Recommendations from the current review focused on three issues evidenced during Year 1. First, the team recommended recutting finance to the FCDO review window, as partner returns used a different review period label and finance had not yet been recut. Second, the team recommended completing menstrual health training in the three remaining schools, reflecting the shortfall on OP2.2, where delivery reached 17 against a target of 20. Third, the team recommended submission of late attendance registers, as four schools submitted registers late and this affected OP1.2 reporting. These actions were grounded in implementation evidence rather than new design changes. [gap:recommendations_and_actions:indicator:recommendations_from_current_review][gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations][fact:indicators.OP2.2.actual][fact:indicators.OP2.2.target]

Updates on previous recommendations showed partial completion. Actions on register cleaning were partly completed, and September deduplication removed double-count risk on OP1.1. This indicated that earlier data quality concerns had been addressed in part, but follow-up remained necessary where source records were still delayed. [gap:recommendations_and_actions:indicator:updates_on_previous_recommendations]

Priorities carried into the next period were therefore clear from this review record: close the OP2.2 gap at 17 out of 20 schools; complete disposal bins at four latrine units; and align reporting period labelling with the award letter. The accompanying action plan assigned these areas to named functions already identified in management follow-up: Programme Manager for recutting the AR1 period by Q1 next period, M&E for chasing four schools for Term 3 registers, and WASH for finishing disposal bins. Exact due dates beyond “Q1 next period” were not available in the submitted records, so they are shown as pending confirmation in the action table narrative rather than stated as fixed dates. [gap:recommendations_and_actions:indicator:priorities_for_next_period][gap:recommendations_and_actions:table:recommendations_action_plan]
assumptions: The required recommendations action table could not be fully populated with exact due dates because submitted records only specified 'Q1 next period' for one action and gave no fixed calendar dates for the others.
Priority and status labels for each table row were not provided in facts or gap answers, so these fields could not be assigned without fabrication.
The source material identified owners as Programme Manager, M&E, and WASH functions, but did not provide individual names.

conflicts.annotation: The proposal states a target of 85% for OP3.3 (hardship grant household attendance follow-up), while the AR1 logframe records 0.75 (i.e. 75%). Even accounting for the possibility that the AR1 figure is a Year 1 sub-target, the numeric values differ (85% vs 75%) and cannot be reconciled by temporal scope alone. Additionally, the proposal uses percentage notation while the logframe uses decimal proportion notation — a unit/format inconsistency that compounds the value difference. Gate-1 review should confirm: (a) whether 0.75 is intentionally a lower Year 1 milestone or an error; (b) whether the proposal figure of 85 is a percentage or has been misrecorded.

content.text:
This Annual Review covered the period 2025-04-01 to 2026-03-31. The programme remained aligned to its stated impact of supporting adolescent girls in Machinga and Mangochi to complete basic education in safer, more supportive learning environments, with the outcome focused on improved retention, attendance and learning continuity by September 2026 [fact:objectives.impact_girls_complete_education; fact:objectives.outcome_improved_school_retention_attendance].

Year 1 delivery remained broadly on track [gap:summary_and_overview:indicator:overall_progress]. Performance against several Year 1 output targets was ahead of plan. The programme reached 684 girls re-enrolled or newly retained against a target of 650 [fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op1_1_girls_reenrolled.actual; fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op1_1_girls_reenrolled.target]. It supported 438 girls to complete at least 20 remedial learning sessions against a target of 420 [fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op1_3_remedial_sessions.actual; fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op1_3_remedial_sessions.target]. It delivered 31 separate, lockable girls' latrine stances against a target of 24 [fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op2_1_latrine_stances.actual; fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op2_1_latrine_stances.target]. It also provided school re-entry kits or learning materials packages to 571 girls against a target of 550, and trained 136 school and community actors on girls' re-entry and safeguarding against a target of 120 [fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op3_2_reentry_kits.actual; fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op3_2_reentry_kits.target; fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op4_3_actors_trained.actual; fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op4_3_actors_trained.target].

Some outputs fell short of Year 1 milestones. Attendance at at least 80% of school days reached 472 girls against a target of 500 [fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op1_2_girls_attendance_80pct.actual; fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op1_2_girls_attendance_80pct.target]. Hardship grants reached 392 caregivers against a target of 400, while verified attendance follow-up was recorded at 0.68 against a target of 0.75 [fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op3_1_hardship_grant_caregivers.actual; fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op3_1_hardship_grant_caregivers.target; fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op3_3_hardship_grant_followup.actual; fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op3_3_hardship_grant_followup.target]. District learning meetings reached three against a target of four [fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op4_1_district_learning_meetings.actual; fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op4_1_district_learning_meetings.target]. Menstrual health support reached 17 schools against a target of 20, and submitted records linked this variance to menstrual health supply delays [fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op2_2_menstrual_health_schools.actual; fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op2_2_menstrual_health_schools.target; gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:new_risks]. A related implementation assumption held in most schools, but three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:realised_assumptions].

The evidence base for reported progress was adequate for routine annual review purposes. Indicator actuals were drawn from the BridgeLight AR1 export, and records included school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists and district validation samples [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:evidence_base_strength; gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:new_evidence]. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures, although late register submission from four schools affected attendance reporting [gap:programme_management_delivery_commercial_financial:indicator:partner_performance; gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations]. No standalone external evaluation was commissioned in Year 1; monitoring relied on termly indicator returns and partner spot checks [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:evaluation_progress].

Financial delivery ran above forecast across the sampled output lines available in the AR1 export. Submitted records stated Year 1 actual spend at GBP 694,860 against forecast GBP 653,000 [gap:programme_management_delivery_commercial_financial:indicator:financial_delivery]. At line level, overspends were recorded on OP1.1 at GBP 174850 against GBP 162000, OP2.1 at GBP 148900 against GBP 121000, OP3.2 at GBP 109250 against GBP 103000, and OP4.3 at GBP 58630 against GBP 54000 [fact:financials.lines.op1_1.actual_year1_gbp; fact:financials.lines.op1_1.budget_yearaerial?]

content.text:
Performance against the programme outcome was positive overall, with stronger delivery on several output areas and some shortfalls in attendance, menstrual health coverage and follow-up verification. The programme outcome aimed for adolescent girls targeted by the programme to demonstrate improved school retention, attendance and learning continuity, with reduced practical and safeguarding barriers to education. Year 1 monitoring reported that attendance and retention improved against Year 1 milestones, using term attendance registers and school safeguarding pathway checks. Evidence was drawn from school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists, and district validation samples.

Delivery against key output targets was mostly on track or above target. Re-enrolment or retention reached 684 girls against a Year 1 target of 650. Completion of at least 20 remedial learning sessions reached 438 girls against a target of 420. Girls receiving school re-entry kits or learning materials reached 571 against a target of 550. Separate lockable girls' latrine stances reached 31 against a target of 24. School and community actors trained on girls' re-entry and safeguarding reached 136 against a target of 120.

A smaller group of indicators fell below Year 1 targets. Girls attending at least 80% of school days reached 472 against a target of 500. Schools with menstrual health supplies and trained focal teachers reached 17 against a target of 20. Caregivers receiving education hardship grants reached 392 against a target of 400. Verified attendance follow-up for hardship grant households reached 0.68 against a logframe target of 0.75. District learning meetings with documented action points reached 3 against a target of 4.

Available evidence explained part of this variance. Four schools submitted attendance registers late, which affected OP1.2 reporting. Menstrual health supply delays affected OP2.2, and three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training. Even so, safeguarding referral pathways were tested in supported schools, and Year 1 monitoring did not report any major incident trend.

The main conclusion from the period is that delivery remained broadly on track, with practical access and school environment outputs performing well and supporting the stated impact that adolescent girls in Machinga and Mangochi complete basic education in safer, more supportive learning environments. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures, which increased confidence in the strongest-performing output data. Monitoring also recorded that previous actions on register cleaning were only partly complete, although September deduplication removed double-count risk on OP1.1.

There were still limits to the evidence base for drawing firmer conclusions at outcome level. No standalone external evaluation was commissioned in Year 1; monitoring relied on termly indicator returns and partner spot checks. The review period used in partner returns was recorded as 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25, while the award letter cited 15-Oct to 14-Oct, and finance had not recut the period at the time of reporting. Exact gender-, age- or vulnerability-disaggregated results were not available in the submitted records for this section.

Overall, the programme delivered credible Year 1 progress toward improved retention, attendance and learning continuity. The strongest results were in re-enrolment, remedial support, re-entry kits, sanitation infrastructure and actor training; the weaker areas were attendance consistency, menstrual health coverage, hardship grant follow-up verification and completion of planned district learning meetings.

content.text:
Monitoring in Year 1 relied on routine programme records rather than a standalone evaluation. Indicator actuals were drawn from the BridgeLight AR1 export, with source notes recorded per output, and attendance and financial lines included variance explanations where available (gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:evidence_base_strength). Submitted evidence comprised school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists, and district validation samples (gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:new_evidence). No standalone external evaluation was commissioned in Year 1; monitoring instead used termly indicator returns and partner spot checks (gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:evaluation_progress).

The evidence base was adequate for assessing several output-level results. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures (gap:programme_management_delivery_commercial_financial:indicator:partner_performance), which supported reported delivery of 684 girls re-enrolled or newly retained against a Year 1 target of 650 (fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op1_1_girls_reenrolled.actual; fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op1_1_girls_reenrolled.target). Routine records also supported reporting that 438 girls completed at least 20 remedial learning sessions against a target of 420 (fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op1_3_remedial_sessions.actual; fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op1_3_remedial_sessions.target), and that 571 girls received school re-entry kits or learning materials against a target of 550 (fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op3_2_reentry_kits.actual; fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op3_2_reentry_kits.target). Physical verification evidence was stronger for infrastructure outputs: WASH-related documentation supported reporting of 31 girls' latrine stances against a target of 24 (fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op2_1_latrine_stances.actual; fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op2_1_latrine_stances.target).

Evidence was weaker where reporting depended on late or incomplete school submissions. Four schools submitted attendance registers late, which affected OP1.2 reporting (gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations). That limitation reduced confidence in the completeness of the attendance result of 472 girls attending at least 80% of school days against a target of 500 (fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op1_2_girls_attendance_80pct.actual; fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op1_2_girls_attendance_80pct.target), although it did not invalidate the direction of travel recorded in partner monitoring. The submitted outcome assessment stated that outcome monitoring used term attendance registers and school safeguarding pathway checks, and that supported girls' attendance and retention improved against Year 1 milestones, with variance notes captured in the AR1 export (gap:performance_and_conclusions:table:outcome_assessment).

There were also clear limits to period consistency. Partner returns used a review period of 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25, while the award letter cited 15-Oct to 14-Oct, and finance had not recut the reporting period at the time of submission (gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations). This means the Annual Review evidence was usable for performance tracking, but period alignment should be treated with caution when comparing across narrative, indicator and finance records.

On weaker-performing indicators, the evidence still allowed a plausible explanation for variance. Menstrual health supply delays affected OP2.2, where reported achievement reached 17 schools against a Year 1 target of 20 (gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:new_risks; fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op2_2_menstrual_health_schools.actual; fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op2_2_menstrual_health_schools.target). A related assumption held in most schools, but three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training (gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:realised_assumptions). Taken together, those records gave a credible reason for under-achievement on that indicator.

Safeguarding evidence was present but limited in depth. Submitted records stated that safeguarding referral pathways were tested in supported schools and that no major incident trend was reported in Year 1 monitoring returns (gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:safeguarding_risk_where_relevant). That supported a basic judgement that safeguarding systems were functioning during the period, but exact incident counts or disaggregation were not available in submitted records.

Overall, the monitoring approach produced enough evidence to assess Year 1 output delivery with moderate confidence. Confidence was higher for re-enrolment, remedial sessions, re-entry kits and latrine construction because those results were backed by routine administrative records and validation materials (gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:new_evidence; gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:evidence_base_strength). Confidence was lower for attendance-sensitive measures because late registers from four schools affected completeness, and lower still for cross-period comparability because reporting windows were not yet aligned to the award letter (gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations).

content.text:
Risk exposure remained broadly stable during the reporting period. No new material risks were reported beyond those already recorded in the grant risk register, although menstrual health supply delays affected OP2.2 performance, with 17 schools reached against a Year 1 target of 20. This shortfall appeared alongside an implementation assumption that focal teachers would be available in supported schools; that assumption held in most schools, but three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training. Together, these issues help explain why OP2.2 finished below target rather than indicating a wider delivery failure. Climate and operating context risks were present but did not stop implementation. Lake-shore transport costs increased for OP1.1, which added pressure to delivery costs in that area. Even so, no major climate shock was reported as having stopped Year 1 delivery. Output delivery under OP1.1 still exceeded its Year 1 target, reaching 684 girls re-enrolled or newly retained against a target of 650. Actual spend on OP1.1 was GBP 174850 against a Year 1 budget of GBP 162000, which is consistent with cost pressure during implementation and should be read alongside the transport issue noted above. Safeguarding controls remained active during the year. Safeguarding referral pathways were tested in supported schools, and Year 1 monitoring returns did not report any major incident trend. Monitoring also used school safeguarding pathway checks as part of outcome tracking. The available records therefore suggest that safeguarding arrangements were functioning as intended during routine delivery, though the submitted evidence did not provide incident counts or disaggregation. [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:safeguarding_risk_where_relevant] [gap:performance_and_conclusions:table:outcome_assessment]

Financial control evidence did not show misuse of funds during the period. No evidence was reported of funds being used other than as intended, and hardship grant controls included deduplication of 16 caregiver records before payment. This points to an active pre-payment check rather than a post hoc correction only after disbursement had taken place. Related output data show that hardship grants reached 392 caregivers against a Year 1 target of 400, while verified attendance follow-up reached 0.68 against a Year 1 target of 0.75, indicating that follow-up control performance lagged behind grant distribution performance and needed continued management attention. Overall, controls appear to have contained the main risks that materialised in Year 1. The principal issues were operational rather than systemic: supply delays affecting OP2.2, focal teacher gaps in three schools, and higher transport costs around lake-shore delivery areas. At the same time, the programme maintained functioning safeguarding checks and payment verification steps, and there was no reported evidence of funds being misused during the period. sections.label: F. Programme Management: Delivery, Commercial and Financial Performance

content.text:
Delivery performance in Year 1 was broadly on track. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures, although late register submission from four schools affected attendance reporting. The programme also held district learning meetings with documented action points. [gap:programme_management_delivery_commercial_financial:indicator:partner_performance][gap:programme_management_delivery_commercial_financial:indicator:FCDO_management_actions]

Across the sampled output lines in the AR1 export, actual spend totalled GBP 694,860 against a forecast of GBP 653,000. content.text:
Recommendations in this Annual Review were driven by the main Year 1 variances and data issues recorded during implementation. Previous review actions on register cleaning were partially complete, and September deduplication removed double-count risk on OP1.1. The current review therefore prioritised three follow-up actions: recutting finance to the FCDO 15-Oct-14-Oct review window, completing menstrual health training in the three remaining schools, and submitting late attendance registers. These actions responded directly to the reporting period mismatch in partner returns, the OP2.2 shortfall of 17 schools reached against a target of 20, and delayed attendance data from four schools. [gap:recommendations_and_actions:indicator:updates_on_previous_recommendations] [gap:recommendations_and_actions:indicator:recommendations_from_current_review] [fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op2_2_menstrual_health_schools.actual] [fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op2_2_menstrual_health_schools.target] [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations]

Priority actions for the next period were set out clearly in the submitted action plan. The Programme Manager was assigned to recut the AR1 period by Q1 next period. M&E was assigned to chase the four schools for Term 3 registers. WASH was assigned to finish disposal bins. The same priorities were reflected in the narrative recommendations: close the OP2.2 gap of 17 out of 20 schools, complete disposal bins at four latrine units, and align reporting period labelling with the award letter. [gap:recommendations_and_actions:table:recommendations_action_plan] [gap:recommendations_and_actions:indicator:priorities_for_next_period] [fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op2_2_menstrual_health_schools.actual] [fact:indicators.ar1_logframe.op2_2_menstrual_health_schools.target]

These recommendations were proportionate to performance during the year. Delivery remained broadly on track overall, but attendance reporting and menstrual health inputs needed corrective action before the next review cycle. The recommendations therefore focused on closing known delivery gaps and tightening reporting accuracy rather than changing programme direction. This Annual Review covered the period 2025-04-01 to 2026-03-31 and assessed progress toward the programme outcome of improved school retention, attendance and learning continuity, contributing to the impact of girls completing basic education in safer learning environments. [fact:objectives.outcome] [fact:objectives.impact]

Year 1 delivery remained broadly on track. Re-enrolment and retention exceeded the AR1 milestone, with 684 girls re-enrolled or newly retained against a target of 650. Remedial learning also performed above plan, with 438 girls completing at least 20 sessions against a target of 420. School safety infrastructure progressed ahead of milestone, with 31 lockable girls latrine stances rehabilitated and functional against a target of 24. Attendance was slightly below plan, reaching 472 girls attending at least 80% of school days against a target of 500. Other output areas showed mixed but generally solid delivery. Menstrual health support reached 17 schools against a target of 20, while hardship grants reached 392 caregivers against a target of 400. School re-entry kits or learning materials reached 571 girls against a target of 550. Verified attendance follow-up within 45 days for hardship grant households reached 0.68 against an AR1 target of 0.75, and district learning meetings reached three against a target of four. Training on girls re-entry and safeguarding exceeded plan, reaching 136 school and community actors against a target of 120. Output scoring for Annual Review 1 was populated from the BridgeLight AR1 export, with proposed scores A-C and variance explanations recorded at indicator row level. This section therefore summarises delivered results against AR1 milestones and notes where variance was evident, while recognising that the submitted records did not provide populated impact weightings, baselines, or risk ratings for each row. [gap:detailed_output_scoring:indicator:output_scores][gap:detailed_output_scoring:table:output_score_table]

Performance under Output 1 was mixed but broadly positive. Girls re-enrolled or newly retained reached 684 against an AR1 target of 650. Girls attending at least 80% of school days reached 472 against a target of 500. Girls completing at least 20 remedial learning sessions reached 438 against a target of 420. Taken together, this showed that re-entry and remedial support exceeded milestone levels, while sustained attendance remained slightly below plan. Late attendance registers from four schools affected OP1.2 reporting, which likely contributed to the shortfall recorded against that indicator. [fact:indicators.OP1.1.actual_ar1][fact:indicators.OP1.1.target_ar1][fact:indicators.OP1.2.actual_ar1][fact:indicators.OP1.2.target_ar1][fact:indicators.OP1.3.actual_ar1][fact:indicators.OP1.3.target_ar1][gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations]

Output 2 showed strong progress on sanitation infrastructure but weaker delivery on menstrual health support coverage. Functional lockable girls' latrine stances reached 31 against a target of 24, exceeding the AR1 milestone. Schools with menstrual health supplies and trained focal teachers reached 17 against a target of 20. Submitted records linked this gap to menstrual health supply delays, and a related assumption held only partly because three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training. [fact:indicators.OP2.1.actual_ar1][fact:indicators.OP2.1.target_ar1][fact:indicators.OP2.2.actual_ar1][fact:indicators.OP2.2.target_ar1][gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:new_risks][gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:realised_assumptions]

Output 3 was close to plan on direct support but below plan on follow-up verification. Caregivers receiving an education hardship grant reached 392 against a target of 400, while girls receiving a school re-entry kit or learning materials reached 571 against a target of 550. Verified attendance follow-up within 45 days reached 0.68 against an AR1 milestone of 0.75, so the follow-up process did not meet the expected level during the period under review. Monitoring records also noted that hardship grant records were deduplicated before payment, and no evidence was reported of funds being used other than as intended. [fact:indicators.OP3.1.actual_ar1][fact:indicators.OP3.1.target_ar1][fact:indicators.OP3.2.actual_ar1][fact:indicators.OP3.2.target_ar1][fact:indicators.OP3.3.actual_ar1][fact:indicators.OP3.3.target_ar1][gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:funds_not_used_as_intended_risk]

Output 4 delivered most planned system-strengthening actions but did not fully meet all milestones. District learning meetings with documented action points reached 3 against a target of 4, while school and community actors trained on girls' re-entry and safeguarding reached 136 against a target of 120. Evidence for these outputs included district validation samples and documented action points from district learning meetings, which supported the reported achievements despite one meeting fewer than planned in AR1. content.text:
Monitoring in Year 1 relied on termly indicator returns and partner spot checks rather than a standalone external evaluation. Indicator actuals were drawn from the BridgeLight AR1 export, with source notes recorded per output, and attendance and financial lines included variance explanations where available [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:evaluation_progress; gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:evidence_base_strength]. Submitted evidence for results verification included school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists, and district validation samples [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:new_evidence].

The evidence base was adequate for reporting against most output indicators, but it was stronger for some results than others. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures, which supported confidence in the reported result that OP1.1 reached 684 girls against a Year 1 target of 650 [gap:programme_management_delivery_commercial_financial:indicator:partner_performance; fact:indicators.OP1.1.actual_ar1; fact:indicators.OP1.1.target_ar1]. Evidence also supported infrastructure delivery under OP2.1, where 31 lockable girls latrine stances were reported against a target of 24, drawing on WASH engineer certificates and AR1 indicator records [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:new_evidence; fact:indicators.OP2.1.actual_ar1; fact:indicators.OP2.1.target_ar1].

Evidence was weaker for attendance-related reporting. Four schools submitted attendance registers late, which affected OP1.2 data completeness [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations]. Reported attendance at the threshold of at least 80% of school days stood at 472 against a Year 1 target of 500, but that result should be read with some caution until late registers were fully reconciled [fact:indicators.OP1.2.actual_ar1; fact:indicators.OP1.2.target_ar1; gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations]. The same limitation reduced confidence in any wider interpretation of short-term attendance performance beyond the reported milestone result.

There was also a reporting-period inconsistency in the submitted records. Partner returns used 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25, while the award letter period cited in the gap answer used 15-Oct to 14-Oct, and finance had not recut the data at the time of review [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations]. This did not invalidate the AR1 dataset, but it did limit strict comparability across narrative, finance and monitoring records in this review cycle [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:evidence_base_strength; gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations].

No standalone evaluation findings were available from an external study in Year 1 [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:evaluation_progress]. As a result, this section assessed progress mainly through routine monitoring evidence rather than independent outcome evaluation. Submitted records still showed consistent signs of delivery across several output areas, including remedial learning participation at 438 against a target of 420, hardship grants to 392 caregivers against a target of 400, school re-entry kits or learning materials to 571 girls against a target of 550, district learning meetings at 3 against a target of 4, and training for school and community actors at 136 against a target of 120 [fact:indicators.OP1.3.actual_ar1; fact:indicators.OP1.3.target_ar1; fact:indicators.OP3.1.actual_ar1; fact:indicators.OP3.1.target_ar1; fact:indicators.OP3.2.actual_ar1; fact:indicators.OP3.2.target_ar1; fact:indicators.OP4.1.actual_ar1; fact:indicators.OP4.1.target_ar1; fact:indicators.OP4.3.actual_ar1; fact:indicators.OP4.3.target_ar1].

Some variance was evident and was explained in submitted records or gap answers. OP2.2 reached 17 schools against a target of 20, and the stated reason was delays in menstrual health supplies [fact:indicators.OP2.2.actual_ar1; fact:indicators.OP2.2.target_ar1; gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:new_risks]. A related implementation constraint was that three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:realised_assumptions]. For OP3.3, follow-up within 45 days reached 0.68 against an AR1 target of 0.75 [fact:indicators.OP3.3.actual_ar1; fact:indicators.OP3.3.target_ar1]. The knowledge bank also flagged a unit-scale issue between the AR1 milestone target and the proposal-level programme target for this indicator, so only the AR1 values were used here.

Overall, the evidence base supported a reasonable Annual Review judgement on Year 1 output delivery, but with clear limits around attendance completeness, period alignment and the absence of external evaluation evidence [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:evidence_base_strength; gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations; gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:evaluation_progress].

content.text:
No new material risks were reported beyond those already recorded in the grant risk register. During the period, one operational issue did affect delivery: menstrual health supply delays contributed to OP2.2 reaching 17 schools against a Year 1 target of 20. The related assumption that community focal teachers would be available held in most schools, but three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training. This helps explain the shortfall on that output and points to an implementation constraint rather than a wider breakdown in programme control. [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:new_risks] [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:realised_assumptions] [fact:indicators.OP2.2.actual_ar1] [fact:indicators.OP2.2.target_ar1]

Climate and operating conditions created some cost pressure but did not stop delivery. Lake-shore transport costs increased for OP1.1, and actual spend on that line was 174850 against a budget of 162000. Even with that variance, delivery on the same output exceeded the Year 1 milestone, with 684 girls re-enrolled or newly retained against a target of 650. No major climate shock was reported as having stopped delivery in Year 1. [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:climate_environment_risk] [fact:financials.lines.OP1.1.actual] [fact:financials.lines.OP1.1.budget] [fact:indicators.OP1.1.actual_ar1] [fact:indicators.OP1.1.target_ar1]

Financial control remained in place during hardship grant delivery. No evidence was reported that funds were used other than as intended, and hardship grant processing removed duplicate risk before payment by deduplicating 16 caregiver records. That control is consistent with the programme reporting 392 caregivers receiving an education hardship grant during AR1. However, follow-up verification within 45 days reached 0.68 against a Year 1 target of 0.75, so control over post-disbursement attendance tracking was weaker than planned even though pre-payment checks were functioning. [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:funds_not_used_as_intended_risk] [fact:indicators.OP3.1.actual_ar1] [fact:indicators.OP3.3.actual_ar1] [fact:indicators.OP3.3.target_ar1]

Safeguarding controls were active during the period. Safeguarding referral pathways were tested in supported schools, and Year 1 monitoring returns did not report any major incident trend. More broadly, school/community actors trained on girls re-entry and safeguarding reached 136 against a Year 1 target of 120, which suggests planned safeguarding-related orientation was delivered at scale. District learning meetings with documented action points also reached three against a target of four, providing an additional route for escalation and follow-up where issues arose. [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:safeguarding_risk_where_relevant] [fact:indicators.OP4.3.actual_ar1] [fact:indicators.OP4.3.target_ar1] [fact:indicators.OP4.1.actual_ar1] [fact:indicators.OP4.1.target_ar1]

Taken together, the risk picture remained manageable during the review period. The main realised issues were delays affecting menstrual health inputs, gaps in female focal teacher availability in three schools, and higher transport costs in lake-shore areas. These issues caused variance on selected outputs but did not amount to new material risks at programme level, and available controls on safeguarding and grant payment remained in use throughout the period. Exact previous and current RAG ratings, named owners, and status entries for a formal risk update table were not available in the submitted records.

content.text:
Value for Money in Year 1 was assessed mainly through spend against AR1 budgets and delivery against AR1 output milestones. Total actual spend reached 920420 against an AR1 budget of 880000, so expenditure was above plan overall during the period [fact:financials.ar1.total_actual; fact:financials.ar1.total_budget]. At line level, overspends were concentrated in activities that also delivered strongly: OP1.1 spent 174850 against 162000 and reached 684 girls re-enrolled or newly retained against a target of 650 [fact:financials.lines.OP1.1.actual; fact:financials.lines.OP1.1.budget; fact:indicators.OP1.1.actual_ar1; fact:indicators.OP1.1.target_ar1]. OP2.1 spent 148900 against 121000 and delivered 31 lockable girls latrine stances against a target of 24 [fact:financials.lines.OP2.1.actual; fact:financials.lines.OP2.1.budget; fact:indicators.OP2.1.actual_ar1; fact:indicators.OP2.1.target_ar1]. This suggests higher unit costs in those areas, but the submitted records did not include business case baselines or cost-driver analysis, so economy could only be judged in relation to delivery achieved rather than to benchmark prices or procurement savings.

Efficiency was mixed across outputs. Several lines combined near-plan spending with results at or above milestone: OP1.3 spent 81330 against 88000 and achieved 438 girls completing at least 20 remedial learning sessions against a target of 420 [fact:financials.lines.OP1.3.actual; fact:financials.lines.OP1.3.budget; fact:indicators.OP1.3.actual_ar1; fact:indicators.OP1.3.target_ar1]. OP3.2 spent 109250 against 103000 and reached 571 girls receiving school re-entry kits or learning materials against a target of 550 [fact:financials.lines.OP3.2.actual; fact:financials.lines.OP3.2.budget; fact:indicators.OP3.2.actual_ar1; fact:indicators.OP3.2.target_ar1]. OP4.3 spent 58630 against 54000 and trained 136 school or community actors against a target of 120 [fact:financials.lines.OP4.3.actual; fact:financials.lines.OP4.3.budget; fact:indicators.OP4.3.actual_ar1; fact:indicators.OP4.3.target_ar1]. By contrast, OP2.2 underspent at 39600 against 42000 but still fell short at 17 schools against a target of 20, with menstrual health supply delays affecting delivery [fact:financials.lines.OP2.2.actual; fact:financials.lines.OP2.2.budget; fact:indicators.OP2.2.actual_ar1; fact:indicators.OP2.2.target_ar1; gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:new_risks]. OP3.3 also underspent at 24980 against 31000 and reached 0.68 against a target of 0.75 for verified attendance follow-up within 45 days [fact:financials.lines.OP3.3.actual; fact:financials.lines.OP3.3.budget; fact:indicators.OP3.3.actual_ar1; fact:indicators.OP3.3.target_ar1]. Data quality issues reduced confidence on some efficiency judgements because four schools submitted attendance registers late, affecting OP1.2 reporting [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations].

Effectiveness was stronger than the aggregate spend variance alone would suggest, because most measured outputs met or exceeded AR1 milestones and outcome monitoring reported improvement in attendance and retention against Year 1 milestones [gap:performance_and_conclusions:table:outcome_assessment]. In Output area 1, OP1.2 reached 472 girls attending at least 80% of school days against a target of 500, while OP1.1 and OP1.3 both exceeded milestone targets [fact:indicators.OP1.2.actual_ar1; fact:indicators.OP1.2.target_ar1; fact:indicators.OP1.,actual_ar?]. Support under Output area ,actual? Wait.

content.text:

The programme held district learning meetings with documented action points, and FCDO management actions were tracked through the review pack process noted in the award letter context. Evidence available for this section did not identify any supplier or consultant performance issue during the period, but no specific supplier performance narrative was provided in submitted records. content.text:
Recommendations in this review were based on the main Year 1 variances and data issues recorded during implementation. The current review recommended recutting finance to the FCDO Annual Review window of 15 October 2024 to 14 October 2025, completing menstrual health training in the three remaining schools, and securing submission of late attendance registers. These actions responded to the reporting-period mismatch between partner returns and the award letter, the OP2.2 shortfall, and delayed attendance data from four schools. Updates on previous recommendations showed partial completion. Earlier action on register cleaning had progressed, and September deduplication removed double-count risk on OP1.1. That finding supported confidence in the reported re-entry result, although attendance reporting still depended on follow-up with late-submitting schools. [gap:recommendations_and_actions:indicator:updates_on_previous_recommendations] [fact:indicators.OP1.1.actual_ar1] [fact:indicators.OP1.1.target_ar1] [gap:programme_management_delivery_commercial_financial:indicator:partner_performance]

Priorities for the next period were clear from Year 1 delivery evidence. The programme needed to close the OP2.2 gap from 17 against a target of 20 schools, complete disposal bins at four latrine units, and align reporting-period labelling with the award letter. The action plan supplied for follow-up assigned responsibility to the Programme Manager to recut the AR1 period by Q1 next period, to M&E to chase four schools for Term 3 registers, and to WASH to finish disposal bins. Exact calendar due dates, priority ratings, and status fields were not available in submitted records. - Recommendation: Submit outstanding attendance documentation from four schools; Owner: M&E; Due date: exact date not available in submitted records; Priority: not specified in submitted records; Status: not specified in submitted records; Follow-up required: chase Term 3 registers and update attendance reporting.
- Recommendation: Complete menstrual health actions in remaining schools and finish disposal bins at four latrine units; Owner: WASH; Due date: exact date not available in submitted records; Priority: not specified in submitted records; Status: not specified in submitted records; Follow-up required: close the OP2.2 gap and finish disposal-bin works. conflicts.annotation: The AR1 logframe expresses the OP3.3 target as 0.75 (likely a ratio, i.e. 75%) while the proposal states 85%. These also differ in period scope (AR1 period vs full programme). Two distinct issues are present: (1) possible unit/representation difference (ratio vs percentage) and (2) a genuine numeric difference even if both were converted to the same unit (75% ≠ 85%). Gate-1 reviewer should confirm whether 0.75 is a ratio equivalent to 75% and whether the numeric gap reflects a revised programme target or a data entry error.
