content.text:
This Annual Review covered the period 2025-04-01 to 2026-03-31. Year 1 delivery remained broadly on track, with stronger performance on re-enrolment, remedial learning, school WASH infrastructure, re-entry materials and training outputs than had been planned for the year, while attendance, menstrual health coverage, hardship grant reach and follow-up, and district learning meetings fell below their Year 1 milestones. The programme outcome remained focused on adolescent girls’ retention, attendance and learning continuity, and the wider impact objective remained adolescent girls completing basic education in safer, more supportive learning environments. [fact:objectives.outcome_girls_retention_attendance_continuity; fact:objectives.impact_girls_complete_basic_education; gap:summary_and_overview:indicator:overall_progress]

Against Output 1, the programme reported 684 girls re-enrolled or newly retained against a Year 1 target of 650. It also reported 472 girls attending at least 80% of school days against a target of 500, and 438 girls completing at least 20 remedial learning sessions against a target of 420. This showed that access and remedial support outputs exceeded plan overall, but sustained attendance lagged behind milestone. Late attendance register submission from four schools affected OP1.2 reporting, which helps explain part of the variance on attendance. [fact:indicators.OP1.1.actual; fact:indicators.OP1.1.target_year1; fact:indicators.OP1.2.actual; fact:indicators.OP1.2.target_year1; fact:indicators.OP1.3.actual; fact:indicators.OP1.3.target_year1; gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations]

Against Output 2, the programme delivered 31 girls’ latrine stances rehabilitated or newly functional against a target of 24. However, only 17 schools had menstrual health supplies and trained focal teachers against a target of 20. Reported variance reflected menstrual health supply delays, and three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training. Safeguarding referral pathways were tested in supported schools, and Year 1 monitoring returns did not report any major incident trend. [fact:indicators.OP2.1.actual; fact:indicators.OP2.1.target_year1; fact:indicators.OP2.2.actual; fact:indicators.OP2.2.target_year1; gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:new_risks; gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:realised_assumptions; gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:safeguarding_risk_where_relevant]

Against Output 3, the programme reached 392 caregivers with an education hardship grant against a target of 400 and provided 571 girls with a school re-entry kit or learning materials package against a target of 550. Verified attendance follow-up within 45 days reached 0.68 against a target of 0.75. Monitoring controls identified no evidence that funds were used other than intended, and hardship grant checks deduplicated 16 caregiver records before payment. [fact:indicators.OP3.1.actual; fact:indicators.OP3.1.target_year1; fact:indicators.OP3.2.actual; fact:indicators.OP3.2.target_year1; fact:indicators.OP3.3.actual; fact:indicators.OP3.3.target_year1; gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:funds_not_used_as_intended_risk]

Against Output 4, the programme held 3 district learning meetings with documented action points against a target of 4 and trained 136 school or community actors on girls’ re-entry and safeguarding protocols against a target of 120. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures, although partner performance on attendance reporting was weakened by late register submission from four schools. Evidence used across outputs included school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists and district validation samples. No standalone external evaluation was commissioned in Year 1; monitoring relied on termly indicator returns and partner spot checks. content.text:
Performance against the programme outcome was positive overall, with Year 1 delivery broadly on track against the agreed output milestones. The programme outcome remained that adolescent girls demonstrate improved school retention, attendance and learning continuity by September 2026. During the review period, supported girls’ attendance and retention improved against Year 1 milestones, based on term attendance registers and school safeguarding pathway checks. Re-enrolment or newly retained girls reached 684 against a Year 1 target of 650. Attendance at 80% or more of school days reached 472 against a target of 500, while girls completing at least 20 remedial learning sessions reached 438 against a target of 420. These results suggest that retention and learning continuity progressed well, although regular attendance lagged slightly behind plan. [fact:objectives.outcome_girls_retention_attendance_continuity; gap:performance_and_conclusions:table:outcome_assessment; fact:indicators.OP1.1.actual; fact:indicators.OP1.1.target_year1; fact:indicators.OP1.2.actual; fact:indicators.OP1.2.target_year1; fact:indicators.OP1.3.actual; fact:indicators.OP1.3.target_year1]

Progress on safer and more supportive learning conditions was mixed but still substantial. The programme delivered 31 girls’ latrine stances rehabilitated or newly functional against a Year 1 target of 24, which exceeded plan. By contrast, schools with menstrual health supplies and trained focal teachers reached 17 against a target of 20. Reported variance was linked to menstrual health supply delays, and records also noted that three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training. Safeguarding referral pathways were tested in supported schools, and Year 1 monitoring did not report a major incident trend. Taken together, this showed that the physical environment improved faster than expected in some areas, while menstrual health readiness remained incomplete in a small number of schools by period end. Household and direct learner support largely met planned levels. Monitoring in Year 1 relied on routine programme data rather than a standalone external evaluation. Submitted records state that outcome monitoring used term attendance registers and school safeguarding pathway checks, while broader monitoring relied on termly indicator returns and partner spot checks. Evidence submitted for verification included school registers, re-entry club forms, WASH engineer certificates, mobile-money hardship grant lists, and district validation samples. Indicator actuals were drawn from the BridgeLight AR1 export, with source notes per output and variance explanations recorded for attendance and financial lines. [gap:performance_and_conclusions:table:outcome_assessment; gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:evaluation_progress; gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:new_evidence; gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:evidence_base_strength]

The evidence base was adequate to assess most output-level delivery, but it was uneven across indicators. District validation samples confirmed re-entry figures, which supported confidence in OP1.1 reporting of 684 against a Year 1 target of 650. Other output results were also traceable through the AR1 export, including OP1.3 at 438 against 420, OP2.1 at 31 against 24, OP3.2 at 571 against 550, and OP4.3 at 136 against 120. These results suggested that several delivery areas met or exceeded their Year 1 milestones in the submitted dataset. [gap:programme_management_delivery_commercial_financial:indicator:partner_performance; fact:indicators.OP1.1.actual; fact:indicators.OP1.1.target_year1; fact:indicators.OP1.3.actual; fact:indicators.OP1.3.target_year1; fact:indicators.OP2.1.actual; fact:indicators.OP2.1.target_year1; fact:indicators.OP3.2.actual; fact:indicators.OP3.2.target_year1; fact:indicators.OP4.3.actual; fact:indicators.OP4.3.target_year1]

There were, however, clear data quality limits that affected confidence in some findings. Partner returns used a review period of 01-Oct-24 to 30-Sep-25, while the award letter cited 15-Oct to 14-Oct, and finance had not recut the period at the time of reporting. In addition, four schools submitted attendance registers late, which affected OP1.2 reporting. That limitation mattered because OP1.2 reported 472 girls attending at least 80% of school days against a Year 1 target of 500, so the shortfall should be read with caution until the missing records are fully reconciled. [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations; fact:indicators.OP1.2.actual; fact:indicators.OP1.2.target_year1]

Evidence for menstrual health and school environment outputs was mixed. The AR1 export recorded OP2.2 at 17 schools against a Year 1 target of 20, and submitted risk information linked this variance to menstrual health supply delays. A related assumption held in most schools but did not hold everywhere: three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training. Taken together, those records provided a plausible explanation for under-delivery on OP2.2, but they also showed that performance depended on timely supplies and staff availability at school level rather than on reporting alone. content.text:
No new material risks were reported beyond those already recorded in the grant risk register. The main delivery issue during the period was delay in menstrual health supplies, which contributed to OP2.2 reaching 17 schools against a Year 1 target of 20. This shortfall was also linked to an assumption that focal teachers would be available in supported schools; that assumption held in most schools, but three schools lacked a female focal teacher for menstrual health training. These factors help explain why menstrual health support lagged while other outputs remained broadly on track. Climate and operating conditions did not stop delivery in Year 1, although lake-shore transport costs increased for OP1.1. That cost pressure sat alongside higher actual spend on OP1.1 of GBP 174850 against a budget of GBP 162000. Records did not provide a fuller breakdown of how much of this variance was attributable to transport alone, so the report treats transport cost inflation as a contributing factor rather than a quantified sole cause. [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:climate_environment_risk] [fact:financials.lines.OP1.1.actual] [fact:financials.lines.OP1.1.budget]

Safeguarding controls remained active during implementation. Safeguarding referral pathways were tested in supported schools, and Year 1 monitoring returns did not report any major incident trend. Related evidence on service readiness remained partial in the submitted records: the proposal included an endline target for schools with a functional safeguarding pathway, but no corresponding AR1 actual was available in the logframe export reviewed for this section. The programme therefore relied on monitoring returns and school checks rather than a completed output result for that indicator in this review period. [gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:safeguarding_risk_where_relevant] [fact:indicators.op2_3_schools_safeguarding_pathway.target_endline]

Financial control measures also operated during the period. There was no evidence that funds were used other than as intended, and hardship grant processes removed duplicate risk by deduplicating 16 caregiver records before payment. This control was relevant to OP3.1, under which 392 caregivers received an education hardship grant against a Year 1 target of 400, while attendance follow-up within 45 days reached 0.68 against a target of 0.75. Taken together, this suggests that payment control functioned, but post-payment follow-up remained weaker than planned and needed continued management attention. Overall, risk management during the period was steady rather than static. Existing risks were monitored, core controls operated, and no new material risk category emerged from Year 1 delivery records. At the same time, supply delays, staffing gaps in three schools, and higher transport costs showed where assumptions were only partly met and where implementation pressure affected results quality or timing rather than stopping delivery altogether. Value for money in Year 1 was assessed from actual delivery against Year 1 milestones and from forecast versus actual output costs. Across the sampled output lines in the AR1 export, actual spend totalled GBP 694,860 against forecast GBP 653,000, showing an overall overspend during the period reviewed. The available records did not provide a completed VfM measures table or separate quantified commentary on cost drivers, economy, efficiency and effectiveness beyond the output and finance lines, so this assessment is based on those lines and the Year 1 results narrative rather than a standalone VfM tool. [gap:programme_management_delivery_commercial_financial:indicator:financial_delivery][gap:value_for_money:table:vfm_measures]

Economy. Spending was above budget on several delivery lines. OP1.1 recorded GBP 174,850 against a budget of GBP 162,000; OP1.2 recorded GBP 98,740 against GBP 94,000; OP2.1 recorded GBP 148,900 against GBP 121,000; OP3.1 recorded GBP 151,440 against GBP 146,000; OP3.2 recorded GBP 109,250 against GBP 103,000; and OP4.3 recorded GBP 58,630 against GBP 54,000. Available evidence linked part of this pressure to increased lake-shore transport costs for OP1.1. At the same time, some lines were delivered below budget: OP1.3 spent GBP 81,330 against GBP 88,000; OP2.2 spent GBP 39,600 against GBP 42,000; OP3.3 spent GBP 24,980 against GBP 31,000; and OP4.1 spent GBP 32,700 against GBP 39,000. On balance, economy was mixed rather than consistently strong: some overspends appear to have supported outputs that exceeded target, while some underspends reflected incomplete delivery or lower activity volume in period. Efficiency. Several outputs met or exceeded their Year 1 milestones despite cost pressure in some lines. Re-enrolment or retention reached 684 girls against a target of 650; remedial learning reached 438 girls against 420; latrine stances reached 31 against 24; school re-entry kits or learning materials reached 571 girls against 550; and training on girls' re-entry and safeguarding protocols reached 136 actors against 120. These results suggest that resources converted into delivery at or above planned levels for much of the portfolio during Year 1. Efficiency was weaker where reporting or implementation bottlenecks reduced conversion of spend into complete results in period. Attendance at eighty per cent or more of school days reached 472 against a target of 500, with late attendance registers from four schools affecting reporting quality for OP1.2. Menstrual health support reached seventeen schools against a target of twenty, and records noted menstrual health supply delays as well as three schools lacking a female focal teacher for training; this points to slower conversion on that line even though spend remained close to budget at GBP 39,600 against GBP 42,000 for OP2.2 and district learning meetings cost less than budget at GBP 32,700 against GBP 39,000 while delivering three meetings against a target of four for OP4.1. sections.label: F. Programme Management: Delivery, Commercial and Financial Performance

content.text:
Delivery in Year 1 was broadly on track, with stronger performance on several output lines and some reporting and implementation issues that need follow-up. Re-entry results exceeded plan: OP1.1 reached 684 girls against a Year 1 target of 650, while district validation samples confirmed the reported re-entry figures. Attendance performance was slightly below plan at 472 girls attending at least 80% of school days against a target of 500, and partner reporting noted that late register submission from four schools affected attendance reporting. Infrastructure delivery also ran ahead on latrine rehabilitation, with 31 stances delivered against a target of 24. Menstrual health support was behind target at 17 schools against a target of 20, with supply delays affecting delivery and three schools lacking a female focal teacher for menstrual health training. District learning meetings were delivered, with documented action points recorded. [fact:indicators.OP1.1.actual, fact:indicators.OP1.1.target_year1, gap:programme_management_delivery_commercial_financial:indicator:partner_performance, fact:indicators.OP1.2.actual, fact:indicators.OP1.2.target_year1, fact:indicators.OP2.1.actual, fact:indicators.OP2.1.target_year1, fact:indicators.OP2.2.actual, fact:indicators.OP2.2.target_year1, gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:new_risks, gap:risk_and_safeguarding:indicator:realised_assumptions, fact:indicators.OP4.1.actual]

Financial delivery across the sampled output lines in the AR1 export totalled GBP 694,860 against forecast GBP 653,000. Variance was mixed by line rather than uniform across the portfolio. Overspends were recorded on OP1.1 at GBP 174,850 against GBP 162,000 budgeted, OP1.2 at GBP 98,740 against GBP 94,000, OP2.1 at GBP 148,900 against GBP 121,000, OP3.1 at GBP 151,440 against GBP 146,000, OP3.2 at GBP 109,250 against GBP 103,000 and OP4.3 at GBP 58,630 against GBP 54,000. Underspends were recorded on OP1.3 at GBP 81,330 against GBP 88,000 budgeted, OP2.2 at GBP 39,600 against GBP 42,000, OP3.3 at GBP 24,980 against GBP 31,000 and OP4.1 at GBP 32,700 against GBP 39,000. Reported cost pressure affected OP1.1 because lake-shore transport costs increased during the year; by contrast, lower spend on OP2.2 aligned with delayed menstrual health supply delivery and incomplete coverage in three schools. [gap:programme_management_delivery_commercial_financial:indicator:financial_delivery, fact:financials.lines.OP1.1.actual, fact:financials.lines.OP1.1.budgetevidence_used = [

Recommendations from the current review focused on correcting reporting alignment and closing the small number of delivery gaps that remained at year end. The review recommended recutting finance to the FCDO review window of 15-Oct to 14-Oct, completing menstrual health training in the three remaining schools, and submitting the late attendance registers. These actions responded directly to evidence that partner returns used a different review period, that OP2.2 closed at 17 schools against a Year 1 target of 20, and that four schools submitted attendance registers late, which affected OP1.2 reporting. [gap:recommendations_and_actions:indicator:recommendations_from_current_review] [fact:indicators.OP2.2.actual] [fact:indicators.OP2.2.target_year1] [gap:evidence_and_evaluation:indicator:data_quality_limitations]

Updates on previous recommendations showed partial progress rather than full closure. Previous actions on register cleaning were partly completed, and September deduplication removed double-count risk on OP1.1. That finding was consistent with district validation samples confirming re-entry figures, while attendance reporting still faced delays from four schools. [gap:recommendations_and_actions:indicator:updates_on_previous_recommendations] [gap:programme_management_delivery_commercial_financial:indicator:partner_performance]

Priorities carried into the next period were therefore specific and limited: close the OP2.2 gap at 17 out of 20 schools, complete disposal bins at four latrine units, and align reporting-period labelling with the award letter. The action plan named owners for these follow-up steps: the Programme Manager was assigned to recut the AR1 period by Q1 next period; M&E was assigned to chase the four schools for Term 3 registers; and WASH was assigned to finish disposal bins. [gap:recommendations_and_actions:indicator:priorities_for_next_period] [gap:recommendations_and_actions:table:recommendations_action_plan]

Overall, the recommendations were proportionate to performance during the period. They addressed data quality and completion issues without obscuring that delivery remained broadly on track in several areas, including OP1.1 at 684 against a Year 1 target of 650 and OP2.1 at 31 against a target of 24. content.text:
Performance during 2026-01-01 to 2026-06-07 was mixed but generally positive against the available output and outcome-related indicator set. Delivery exceeded target on several indicators. OP1.1 reached 684 against a target of 650, OP1.3 reached 438 against 420, OP2.1 reached 31 against 24, OP3.2 reached 571 against 550, and OP4.3 reached 136 against 120. These results suggested stronger-than-planned delivery in parts of Output 1, Output 2, Output 3 and Output 4 during the period cited. Output delivery was mixed across the reporting period, with several indicators exceeding their logframe targets while others fell short. Evidence available in the submitted logframe data showed stronger performance under Output 1 and parts of Outputs 2, 3 and 4, but the records did not provide confirmed baselines, milestones, impact weightings, risk ratings or output scores for inclusion in a complete scoring table. As a result, this section set out the achieved results and variance against target, but it did not assign formal output scores. Under Output 1, actual achievement exceeded target on two of the three reported indicators. The programme reported 684 against a target of 650 for OP1.1, and 438 against a target of 420 for OP1.3. OP1.2 reached 472 against a target of 500, indicating a modest shortfall on that attendance-related measure. This pattern suggested that re-enrolment or retention support and remedial learning delivery performed ahead of plan, while sustained attendance lagged behind target within the same output area. The variance was therefore narrow on two indicators and positive on one indicator, which suggested that implementation remained close to plan overall even though not all measures met their expected level during the period. content.text:
Value for Money was assessed against the 4Es using available output and spend data for the reporting period. The evidence base supported a partial assessment only. It showed where resources were spent and what output volumes were reported, but it did not include approved budget lines, business case benchmarks, unit-cost assumptions, procurement records, or disaggregation needed for a fuller judgement.

On economy, the programme reported actual spend across multiple output lines: Output 1 line items recorded GBP 174,850, GBP 98,740 and GBP 81,330; Output 2 line items recorded GBP 148,900 and GBP 39,600; Output 3 line items recorded GBP 151,440, GBP 109,250 and GBP 24,980; and Output 4 line items recorded GBP 32,700 and GBP 58,630. These figures showed where expenditure was incurred across delivery components rather than a single concentration in one area. However, submitted records did not provide budget comparators or commercial benchmarks for these same lines. As a result, the review could confirm actual expenditure by component but could not test whether goods or services were purchased at lower cost than expected or whether forecast and actual costs diverged materially.

On efficiency, the evidence suggested that spending translated into sizeable reported output volumes in several areas. For example, under Output 1 the programme reported actuals of 684 for OP1.1, 472 for OP1.2 and 438 for OP1.3 alongside the three Output 1 spend lines noted above. Under Output 3 it reported actuals of 392 for OP3.1, 571 for OP3.2 and 68 for OP3.3 with associated spend of GBP 151,440, GBP 109,250 and GBP 24,980. Outputs with lower absolute volumes also had lower associated spend in some cases: Output 4 reported an actual of 3 for OP4.1 and 136 for OP4.3 with spend of GBP 32,700 and GBP 58,630 respectively. This pattern indicated that resources were linked to delivery activity across all four outputs. Even so, no verified unit-cost analysis was available in submitted records, so efficiency could only be assessed at a high level rather than through confirmed cost-per-result comparisons.

On effectiveness, the programme reported delivery across all available output indicators in the logframe extract: OP1.1 at 684; OP1.2 at 472; OP1.3 at 438; OP2.1 at 31; OP2.2 at 17; OP3.1 at 392; OP3.2 at 571; OP3.3 at 68; OP4.1 at 3; and OP4.3 at 136. That showed that funded activities generated measurable outputs during the period rather than recording spend without results. However, target values were not available in the submitted evidence set used here for these indicators, so the review could not explain variance against target or judge whether performance represented over- or under-achievement.

On equity, the business case material indicated that equity was intended to be assessed through reach among girls with disabilities, ultra-poor girls and out-of-school girls. That gave a clear direction of travel for VfM assessment from an inclusion perspective. But no quantified disaggregation was available in the submitted records used for this section. The review therefore could not verify whether spending reached those groups in line with expectation.

Overall, Value for Money evidence was mixed but usable in part. The programme demonstrated reported outputs against each available output area and documented actual expenditure across corresponding delivery lines. The main limitation was not lack of activity data but lack of comparator data: no approved budget baselines, no forecast-versus-actual tables for the same lines, no commercial evidence on prices paid, and no beneficiary disaggregation to test equity.

sections.label: F. Programme Management: Delivery, Commercial and Financial Performance

content.text:
Delivery during the period showed mixed financial and output performance across the programme. Under Output 1, actual delivery recorded 684 for OP1.1, 472 for OP1.2 and 438 for OP1.3. Spend against the related budget lines was above plan for OP1.1 at GBP 174,850 against GBP 162,000 and for OP1.2 at GBP 98,740 against GBP 94,000, while OP1.3 spent GBP 81,330 against GBP 88,000. This suggested that delivery under this output was largely maintained, but with cost pressure on some activities and lower than planned spend on remedial learning sessions. Output 2 also showed overspend on one line and underspend on another. Actual delivery recorded 31 for OP2.1 and 17 for OP2.2. Financially, OP2.1 spent GBP 148,900 against a budget of GBP 121,000, while OP2.2 spent GBP 39,600 against GBP 42,000. The main variance was therefore concentrated in OP2.1, where spend exceeded plan by a wide margin based on submitted records; however, the source pack did not provide narrative explanation for that variance.
